title: AWS Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02)
description: Exam-style questions for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) exam covering cloud concepts and economics, security and compliance, AWS global infrastructure and core services, and billing, pricing, and support.

domains.name: 1.0 Cloud Concepts
subdomains: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud

domains.name: 3.0 Cloud Technology and Services
subdomains: 3.1 - Deploying and operating in the cloud

questions.question: A team provisions 150 vCPU against a 100 vCPU peak forecast and averages 15% utilization. Which pair of figures does this illustrate?
options: 20%-50% over-provisioning versus peak-predicted demand, and 12%-18% typical on-premises utilization: roughly 85% of the fleet idle
Elasticity working as designed, with 85% of capacity absorbed by auto scaling
A rightsizing success: 15% utilization means the estate is correctly sized
A Spot-instance discount of up to 90% applied to on-demand capacity
questions.explanation: AWS documents on-premises procurement as 20%-50% over peak-predicted demand and average server utilization of 12%-18% (with 'under 15%' cited for on-premises data centers). 150 x 0.15 = 22.5 vCPU of useful work, so about 127.5 vCPU (85%) is idle but still paid for: the argument behind 'stop guessing capacity' and behind rightsizing.

questions.question: An executive asks why the AWS Cloud can offer lower pay-as-you-go prices than a single company building its own data center. Which statement BEST matches the AWS wording?
options: AWS passes volume discounts on because usage from hundreds of thousands of customers is aggregated in the cloud, producing massive economies of scale
AWS charges less than cost for compute during off-peak hours
AWS reuses decommissioned hardware from other customers without warranty
AWS avoids paying for power and cooling in Regions where energy is cheap
questions.explanation: The six advantages state that usage from hundreds of thousands of customers is aggregated in the cloud, and that this lets AWS offer lower pay-as-you-go prices: economies of scale are structural, not a promotion. The other options invent mechanisms AWS does not describe.

questions.question: Capital One reports that it 'reduced the average time needed to build a development environment from 3 months to only minutes' after going all in on AWS. In Task 3.1 terms, which explanation matches the skill the exam tests?
options: The workload became a repeatable process: environments are provisioned the same way on demand instead of assembled by hand as one-time operations
The company adopted multi-cloud, so a second provider could build the development environments in parallel
The team switched to one-time Console operations, because the AWS Management Console is the most common access method
AWS took over application optimization, so the environment no longer had to be built at all
questions.explanation: The exam-guide skill is to 'evaluate requirements to determine whether to use one-time operations or repeatable processes'. A bespoke, hand-built environment takes as long as the queue and the clicking take; the same environment produced by a repeatable process takes minutes: which is AWS's own IaC argument that you 'write your IaC code once and deploy that same code to hundreds of environments in a fraction of the time'. Multi-cloud needs two or more third-party public providers (Capital One runs on AWS only), the Console suits one-time visual work and would not shrink a 3-month queue, and application optimization never moves to AWS in any column of the responsibility matrix. Figures are AWS-published, customer-claimed, accessed Oct 2026.

questions.question: A product team proposes launching Amazon EC2 instances at an AWS edge location so users in remote cities get the lowest possible latency. A solutions architect objects. Which explanation matches AWS documentation as of Oct 2026?
options: Yes: every edge location is a small Region with at least three Availability Zones, so any instance type runs there
No: edge locations were retired in 2026, and CloudFront now caches only inside Availability Zones
Yes: Global Accelerator runs 130 edge points that accept EC2 launches for anycast workloads
No: edge locations give latency and offload for content delivery only; compute runs in Regions and their Availability Zones
questions.explanation: The dossier states that the benefits of edge locations are latency and offload for delivery only, and that you cannot launch an EC2 instance at an edge location (CloudFront 750+ PoPs and Global Accelerator 130 PoPs, as of Oct 2026). Option B confuses tiers: the minimum of three isolated, physically separate Availability Zones belongs to a Region, not an edge location. Option C is numeric bait: the true 130 figure is Global Accelerator PoPs, which route traffic rather than host instances. Option D is a stale-version trap: edge locations are current, which is why CloudFront still counts 750+ of them.

questions.question: A startup writes an internal glossary so its engineers stop mixing four words that the exam keeps apart. Which statements in the glossary are correct?
options: Elasticity means capacity grows AND shrinks automatically as demand changes
Scalability is the ability to handle growth, with no requirement to shrink
High availability is reached by spanning multiple Availability Zones to survive a component failure
Agility is a service a team buys, priced per provisioned unit
Global reach equals high availability, because both words suggest redundancy
Agility means deployment time falls from seconds to milliseconds
questions.explanation: The dossier keeps four words apart: elasticity is grow AND shrink automatically, scalability is growth only, high availability is surviving a component failure using multiple Availability Zones, and agility is provisioning speed from weeks to just minutes. Option D fails because agility is an organizational benefit, not a service: teams iterate because the cost of a failed trial is metered. Option E fails because global reach means going global in minutes across Regions, while cross-Region redundancy is disaster recovery, not high availability. Option F fails on the wording: speed of deployment is published as 'from weeks to just minutes' and must never be quoted as seconds.

questions.question: An analyst refreshes a slide deck of AWS platform and pricing claims before an internal briefing. Which statements are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: AWS offers over 1,000 fully featured services
Amazon S3 launched on 14 March 2006 at 15 cents per gigabyte
Code written for S3 in 2006 must be rewritten before it runs today
AWS's March 2026 post puts S3 at slightly over 2 cents per gigabyte, roughly 85 percent lower
AWS describes the platform as offering over 200 fully featured services
Speed of deployment is published as seconds, not minutes
questions.explanation: The dossier records the S3 launch on 14 March 2006 at 15 cents per gigabyte, the March 2026 post at slightly over 2 cents per gigabyte (about an 85 percent reduction, as of Oct 2026, verify current pricing before use), and AWS's wording of over 200 fully featured services. Option A is the designed numeric bait: the dossier says a claim of over 1,000 services is easy to eliminate. Option C reverses the fact: the S3 code written in 2006 still works unchanged. Option F repeats the seconds trap, since deployment time is published as weeks to just minutes.

questions.question: A study group is rehearsing the six advantages of cloud computing in the order AWS publishes them. Which sequence is correct for the cards on the table?
options: Go global in minutes
Stop guessing capacity
Trade fixed expense for variable expense
Minimize the environmental impact of cloud workloads
Benefit from massive economies of scale
Increase speed and agility
questions.explanation: The dossier publishes the fixed order: trade fixed expense for variable expense, then benefit from massive economies of scale, then stop guessing capacity, then increase speed and agility, then stop spending money running and maintaining data centers, then go global in minutes. The five keyed cards therefore read 2, 4, 1, 5, 0 in that published order. The distractor card (index 3) is not one of the six: minimizing environmental impact is the Well-Architected Sustainability pillar vocabulary, which is a different list entirely. Two further traps: 'go global in minutes' is last in the published list even though it sits first on the table, and 'stop guessing capacity' is third, not first, so a card layout never decides the answer.

questions.question: An instructor builds a flash-card deck of the dated global-infrastructure numbers for Domain 1. Match each statement to the figure AWS published as of Oct 2026.
prompts: Number of AWS Regions as of Oct 2026
Number of Availability Zones as of Oct 2026
Minimum AZs inside every AWS Region
Maximum distance between AZs in a Region
Announced but not yet open as of Oct 2026
options: 39 Regions
Three isolated, physically separate AZs
Two announced Regions: Saudi Arabia and Chile
Within 100 km (60 miles)
124 Availability Zones
questions.explanation: As of Oct 2026 the dossier lists 39 Regions and 124 Availability Zones, each Region carrying a minimum of three isolated, physically separate AZs all within 100 km (60 miles) of each other, with plans for 2 more Regions (Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and Chile) and 7 more AZs announced but not yet open. Every card is a dated figure, so each answer keeps its Oct 2026 label. The plausible mis-cards are the announced Regions, which students read as already open, and the AZ minimum of three, which is easily confused with the 100 km distance because both describe AZ layout inside one Region.

questions.question: A finance lead objects that moving a project to the AWS Cloud still means buying machines months before anyone uses them. Which answer matches AWS wording for this change in spending?
options: You pay only when you consume computing resources, so a fixed expense becomes a variable expense that follows usage
Usage from hundreds of thousands of customers is aggregated, so every customer is charged one discounted rate
Capacity appears on demand with only a few minutes' notice, so no forecast is ever needed
Hardware is purchased once, depreciated over about five years, and refreshed on the same cycle in the cloud
questions.explanation: The first of the six advantages is trade fixed expense for variable expense, whose trigger phrase is pay only when you consume computing resources: buying hardware before you need it is exactly the fixed expense the cloud removes. Option B is the second advantage, aggregation for lower pay-as-you-go prices, which answers a pricing question rather than a timing-of-spend question. Option C is the third advantage, stopping capacity guesses, and it speaks to forecasting, not to fixed versus variable bills. Option D reverses the direction: the purchase-and-refresh cycle is the on-premises habit, and AWS never sells you hardware to depreciate.

questions.question: A capacity planner wants to buy 30 percent more hardware than the peak forecast so a sales event can never take the site down. What does AWS recommend instead?
options: Keep the buffer and size it at 20 percent over the peak, which is the figure AWS recommends for cloud fleets
Provision capacity on demand with only a few minutes' notice instead of buying against the peak forecast
Rightsize the current on-premises estate first, then order the smaller machines in bulk
Lock the guess in with a three-year commitment so the unused capacity still costs less
questions.explanation: The third advantage, stop guessing capacity, is to provision on demand with only a few minutes' notice instead of buying against the forecast, because the on-premises habit is buying 20% to 50% over peak-predicted demand. Option A turns that on-premises habit into an AWS recommendation, which the dossier never states. Option C is rightsizing, a separate Domain 1 lever that shrinks waste after a purchase has already been made. Option D is a commitment discount: it lowers the price of the guess without removing the guess, and a discount on the wrong quantity still buys waste.

questions.question: A product director wants teams to try small ideas and drop the ones that fail without a large write-off. Which benefit does AWS say this delivers, and why?
options: Elasticity, because capacity grows and shrinks automatically as demand changes
High availability, because a failed trial is absorbed by spare capacity in a second Availability Zone
Agility, because teams iterate when the cost of a failed trial is metered rather than sunk
Massive economies of scale, because frequent trials cost less at AWS purchasing volumes
questions.explanation: The dossier defines agility as an organizational benefit: teams iterate because the cost of a failed trial is metered, not sunk, so abandoning a trial costs only what it consumed. Option A defines elasticity correctly, but elasticity answers a demand curve, not a write-off question. Option B is high availability, which answers component failure and is achieved by spanning multiple Availability Zones. Option D is the aggregation argument about unit prices, and the stem mentions no price at all. Agility is also never a service a team buys.

questions.question: A data center team spends its week racking, stacking and powering servers for applications that never change. Which published advantage does moving those applications to the AWS Cloud remove?
options: Trade fixed expense for variable expense, because the machines are replaced by a usage charge
Benefit from massive economies of scale, because AWS buys servers at volume
Stop guessing capacity, because the provider sizes the fleet on your behalf
Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
questions.explanation: The fifth advantage is stop spending money running and maintaining data centers, and the dossier names exactly the work in the stem: racking, stacking, and powering servers. Option A is the first advantage and it governs the timing of spend, not who performs the manual work. Option B is the second advantage, which explains AWS's low unit prices rather than removing an operations workload. Option C is the third advantage, which addresses forecasts, and the provider never sizes a fleet that you own.

questions.question: Two customers of one provider hit their demand peaks in opposite seasons. A colleague models the hardware each would need alone and together. Which statements in the model hold?
options: Covering both peaks with separate hardware would take 20 units of capacity
Combined demand across the two peaks needs only 12 units of hardware
The shared fleet uses 40 percent less hardware for identical demand
The saving is a limited-time promotion the provider withdraws after the first year
Merging the two accounts doubles the requirement to 40 units of hardware
Each customer must still buy 20 units, because cloud accounts cannot share capacity
questions.explanation: The dossier's worked example gives each customer a 10-unit peak, so separate fleets would need 20 units while the two anti-correlated peaks combine into 12 units of demand, which is 40 percent less hardware for identical demand: advantage two as arithmetic. Option D fails because the dossier calls the advantage structural, not a promotion. Option E invents a doubling the model never produces. Option F contradicts the point of the example, because shared capacity is what lets the combined fleet need 12 units rather than 20.

questions.question: A review board checks the sentences about redundancy and location in a proposal before approving it. Which statements hold?
options: High availability comes from spreading one workload across several Regions
Global reach means deploying to multiple AWS Regions without building your own facilities
Global reach and high availability are the same benefit under two different names
High availability is achieved by spanning multiple Availability Zones inside one Region
Redundancy across Regions is disaster recovery, not high availability
Each AWS Region runs in exactly one Availability Zone, so global reach guarantees availability
questions.explanation: The dossier keeps three ideas apart: global reach is go global in minutes across Regions without building facilities, high availability is achieved by spanning multiple Availability Zones, and redundancy across Regions is disaster recovery. Option A reverses the mapping, because cross-Region spread is the disaster-recovery move. Option C collapses two benefits the exam deliberately separates. Option F is numeric bait: each Region carries a minimum of three isolated, physically separate AZs within 100 km of each other as of Oct 2026, so exactly one is false and availability never follows from geography alone.

questions.question: A manager wants three waiting periods placed on a timeline from the longest wait to the shortest. Which sequence of cards is correct?
options: Just minutes: how long cloud deployment takes after the improvement
Seconds: the figure AWS publishes for speed of deployment
6 to 9 months: the on-premises procurement lead time being replaced
Weeks: how long cloud deployment took before the improvement
questions.explanation: The dossier gives two comparisons: on-premises procurement lead times of six to nine months, and a cloud deployment time that drops from weeks to just minutes, so the timeline runs 6 to 9 months, then weeks, then just minutes, which is cards 2, 3, 0. The card at index 1 is the distractor and sits outside the timeline, because speed of deployment must never be quoted as seconds: the published wording is from weeks to just minutes. The cards are shuffled, so position on the table never signals position in the sequence.

questions.question: An architect maps each stated need to one of the headline benefits in Task 1.1. Match each need to the benefit that answers it.
prompts: New environments take weeks and the queue must collapse to minutes
Users far from the Region need lower latency without new facilities
A single failed component must not take the service down
Traffic doubles overnight and must shrink again by morning
A failed trial should cost only what it consumed, so teams keep trying
options: Elasticity
Global reach
Agility
Speed of deployment
High availability
questions.explanation: Task 1.1 lists the benefits of global infrastructure (speed of deployment, global reach) and the advantages of high availability, elasticity and agility, and each need selects one: an environment queue measured in weeks is speed of deployment; serving distant users without new facilities is global reach; surviving a component failure is high availability; growing and then shrinking with overnight traffic is elasticity; a cheap-to-abandon trial is agility. The closest mis-card is agility for the first prompt, because both carry weeks-to-minutes wording, but the stem's noun decides: an environment queue is deployment time, while iteration after a metered failure is the organizational benefit.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A Python team wants to define cloud infrastructure in code but still have AWS provision and configure it natively. Which pairing is correct?
options: AWS CDK: it defines infrastructure in code and provisions it through AWS CloudFormation, in languages including Python
AWS CloudShell: it runs Python interactively against the AWS APIs
HashiCorp Terraform; because it is the only AWS-native infrastructure-as-code framework
AWS Elastic Beanstalk; because it compiles Python into a CloudFormation template
questions.explanation: AWS CDK is 'an open-source software development framework for defining cloud infrastructure in code and provisioning it through AWS CloudFormation', with TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C#/.NET and Go supported (six languages as of Oct 2026). CDK synthesizes a CloudFormation template: it does not rival it. CloudShell is out of scope, Terraform is third-party and platform agnostic (absent from the in-scope list), and Elastic Beanstalk deploys application code rather than compiling infrastructure.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A platform team must apply an identical networking change every month across 20 AWS accounts, and the change must be auditable. Which approach does Task 3.1 expect?
options: AWS Management Console, because it is the most common method and shows the change visually
AWS CloudShell, because a browser shell can script the change across accounts
Infrastructure as code with AWS CloudFormation, because the process is repeatable and the template is a text file you can track and diff
Amazon EC2, because the change can be made from an instance in each account
questions.explanation: The exam-guide skill is to evaluate whether to use one-time operations or repeatable processes. Monthly change across 20 accounts is the definition of repeatable, and AWS says IaC makes environments 'repeatable, reliable, and consistent' and lets you 'write your IaC code once and deploy that same code to hundreds of environments'. The Console suits one-time work, not standardized repetition. CloudShell is on the out-of-scope list, and EC2 is not an access method at all.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: Keeping three hot spare instances idle so a failure never reaches users will be judged how by the Well-Architected pillars?
options: It has no pillar impact; spare capacity is an operations-only concern
It improves Reliability while worsening Cost Optimization: the pillars trade off and are not interchangeable
It improves Sustainability because idle instances consume no power
It improves Security and Cost Optimization simultaneously
questions.explanation: Task 1.2 tests 'identifying differences between the pillars'. Spare capacity raises Reliability (failure is absorbed) and lowers Cost Optimization (illustrative 400 USD/month = 4,800 USD/year as of Oct 2026: a teaching figure, not an AWS list price: buys nothing). There is no universally winning pillar: the exam wants a deliberate, measured trade-off.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: Which statement about the AWS Well-Architected Framework is correct?
options: A Well-Architected review is an audit mechanism you pass or fail, and the Well-Architected Tool is billed per review
It documents best practices for secure, reliable, efficient, cost-effective and sustainable workloads; the review is a constructive conversation, and the Well-Architected Tool is free
Its six pillars are Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations
Its pillars must be satisfied in order, beginning with Cost Optimization
questions.explanation: AWS describes the Framework as best practices for secure, reliable, efficient, cost-effective and sustainable workloads, and states a review is 'a constructive conversation ... not an audit mechanism'. The Tool is free and in scope. Option C lists the AWS CAF perspectives, not the Well-Architected pillars, and no pillar has priority.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A reviewer notices that her notes mix three different AWS lists. Which statements correctly keep the three lists apart?
options: The Well-Architected Framework lists six pillars that judge the quality of a workload
The AWS CAF lists six perspectives that judge organizational readiness
The Cloud Value Framework has five pillars, and cost savings is only the first of the five
Governance is a Well-Architected pillar that sits alongside Security and Reliability
Sustainability is one of the six AWS CAF perspectives
Scalability is one of the six Well-Architected pillars
questions.explanation: The dossier warns that three lists are never to mix: Well-Architected 6 pillars (workload quality), AWS CAF 6 perspectives (Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security, Operations: organizational readiness), and the Cloud Value Framework 5 pillars, where cost savings (TCO) is only pillar 1 of 5. Option D fails because Governance exists only in the CAF; the six pillars are Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability. Option E fails for the mirror reason: Sustainability is a Well-Architected pillar, not a CAF perspective. Option F is a designed distractor from the dossier: scalability is a Domain 1 cloud benefit, never one of the six pillars.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: An SRE team is rewriting its reliability playbook and wants every line traceable to the Well-Architected reliability design principles as of Oct 2026. Which statements belong in that playbook?
options: Configure the workload to recover from failure automatically
Test recovery procedures instead of assuming they work
Scale horizontally to increase aggregate workload availability
Scale vertically first, because vertical scaling is the published principle
Skip recovery testing in production, because testing risks the customer
Design for zero downtime, because the framework promises uninterrupted service
questions.explanation: The dossier's five reliability design principles as of Oct 2026 are: automatically recover from failure; test recovery procedures; scale horizontally to increase aggregate workload availability; stop guessing capacity; and manage change through automation, all framed by Werner Vogels's 'Everything fails, all the time' and the need to remove single points of failure. Option D inverts the published wording: the principle is horizontal scaling, which raises aggregate availability. Option E contradicts 'test recovery procedures' outright. Option F is an over-claim: the framework prepares a workload for failure rather than promising uninterrupted service, and availability is a shared responsibility.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A platform team turns the Well-Architected general design principles into a wall chart. Which sequence matches the published order for the cards shown?
options: Consider evolutionary architectures
Buy capacity against a three-year forecast
Stop guessing your capacity needs
Test systems at production scale
Automate with architectural experimentation in mind
questions.explanation: The dossier publishes the six general design principles in this order: stop guessing your capacity needs, test systems at production scale, automate with architectural experimentation in mind, consider evolutionary architectures, drive architectures using data, improve through game days. The four keyed cards therefore run 2, 3, 4, 0. The distractor at index 1 is the habit each principle replaces: the dossier says all six principles convert upfront, fixed, idle spend into metered, on-demand, evidence-driven spend, so buying capacity against a forecast is what 'stop guessing your capacity needs' exists to end. The card layout is shuffled, so position on the chart never signals position in the list.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: During a Well-Architected workshop each participant describes one worry in plain language. Match each worry to the pillar that owns it.
prompts: Run, monitor and continually improve the workload
Protect confidentiality, integrity and availability of systems
Do what the workload should do and recover from failure
Use computing resources efficiently as needs change
Avoid unnecessary cost across the workload
Minimize the environmental impact of cloud workloads
options: Operational Excellence
Reliability
Sustainability
Security
Cost Optimization
Performance Efficiency
questions.explanation: The dossier maps the six pillars to what they protect: Operational Excellence runs, monitors and continually improves the workload including automating change and response; Security protects information and systems; Reliability does what the workload is supposed to do and recovers quickly from failure; Performance Efficiency uses computing resources efficiently as demand, technology and business requirements change; Cost Optimization avoids unnecessary cost; Sustainability minimizes environmental impact. The two confusion pairs are deliberate: Security and Reliability both sound like 'resilience', while Sustainability and Cost Optimization both talk about reduction, so the stem's wording decides the pillar. 'Right-sized spend' and 'lower total cost of ownership' are values delivered by Performance Efficiency and Cost Optimization respectively, not spare pillars.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A product team must report the environmental impact of its cloud workload, and the report needs the pillar the framework attaches to that goal. Which pillar owns it, and what value does it deliver?
options: Sustainability: it minimizes the environmental impact of running cloud workloads and delivers ESG performance
Cost Optimization: it minimizes spend, and lower spend always delivers ESG performance
Governance: it is the Well-Architected pillar that owns environmental targets
Scalability: it is the pillar that tracks how workload demand grows
questions.explanation: The six pillars include Sustainability, which minimizes the environmental impact of running cloud workloads, and the dossier maps that pillar to ESG performance. Option B is the designed confusion pair: Sustainability and Cost Optimization both talk about reduction, but only Sustainability owns environmental impact, and cost savings never automatically produce ESG performance. Option C mixes lists, because Governance is an AWS CAF perspective for organizational readiness and never a Well-Architected pillar. Option D is the dossier's named bait: scalability is a Domain 1 cloud benefit, not one of the six pillars.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: Demand, technology and business requirements keep shifting, and a team must keep using computing resources efficiently throughout. Which pillar answers that need, and which value does the framework attach to it?
options: Cost Optimization: it avoids unnecessary cost and delivers a lower total cost of ownership
Performance Efficiency: it uses computing resources efficiently as demand, technology and business requirements change, and it delivers right-sized spend
Reliability: it delivers resilience and is measured by how little computing capacity the workload consumes
Operational Excellence: it delivers right-sized spend by automating every capacity change
questions.explanation: The dossier defines Performance Efficiency as using computing resources efficiently as demand, technology and business requirements change, and it maps that pillar to right-sized spend. Option A is a true sentence about a different pillar: lower total cost of ownership belongs to Cost Optimization, and a total-cost conversation never mentions a shifting demand curve. Option C hands Reliability a cost value, while Reliability delivers resilience. Option D gives Operational Excellence the right-sized-spend value, but that value belongs to Performance Efficiency; Operational Excellence delivers agility and staff productivity.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A platform team is looking for the pillar whose scope covers running, monitoring and continually improving the workload, including automating change and response. Which pillar is it?
options: Operations: it is one of the six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework
Reliability: it does what the workload is supposed to do and recovers quickly from failure
Operational Excellence: it runs, monitors and continually improves the workload, including automating change and response
Performance Efficiency: it uses computing resources efficiently as demand and technology change
questions.explanation: The dossier maps Operational Excellence to running, monitoring and continually improving the workload, including automating change and response, so the stem's wording is that pillar's scope verbatim. Option A mixes lists: Operations is an AWS CAF perspective, while the pillar is named Operational Excellence. Option B is a true statement about Reliability, but recovery from failure answers a different pain from continual improvement. Option D is likewise true about Performance Efficiency, whose scope is efficient use of computing resources as requirements change, not improving the run phase.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A colleague argues that because designing cloud architecture is listed as an out-of-scope job task, Task 1.2 cannot ask candidates to name anything architectural. How should you reply?
options: Task 1.2 was rewritten after CLF-C01 and no longer mentions the Well-Architected Framework
Task 1.2 expects a fully drawn architecture diagram, which is graded for correctness
Out-of-scope tasks never appear in any question, so pillar names are unexaminable
Task 1.2 still asks you to name the Well-Architected pillars: the exam tests principles and recognition, not drawings
questions.explanation: The dossier calls this the scope paradox: designing cloud architecture is an out-of-scope job task, yet Task 1.2 still asks you to name the Well-Architected pillars, because the exam tests selection and recognition and never asks you to build or debug. Option A is a stale-version trap: the domain weights have not moved since CLF-C02 went live on 19 September 2023, and Task 1.2 keeps the framework. Option B over-claims in the other direction, since no item asks for a drawing. Option C is the mirror over-claim: out-of-scope tasks still feed distractors, and naming the pillars is explicitly examinable.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A facilitator asks study groups what the six general design principles have in common. Which statements hold?
options: Every principle must be applied in the order the six pillars are listed
They convert upfront, fixed, idle spend into metered, on-demand, evidence-driven spend
Capacity has to be bought before it is needed, which is their shared purpose
The habit each one replaces runs from buying for a forecast peak to hoping failure never happens
Each principle exists only to lower the monthly bill and has no effect on workload quality
Improve through game days closes the published list of six principles
questions.explanation: The dossier states the common move twice: all six principles convert upfront, fixed, idle spend into metered, on-demand, evidence-driven spend, and the habit each one replaces runs from buying for a forecast peak to hoping failure never happens. Improve through game days is the sixth principle in the published order, so option F belongs. Option A invents a priority order that Task 1.2 denies, because no pillar has priority. Option C states the habit the principles exist to end rather than the purpose they serve. Option E narrows all six to billing, but they also drive workload quality and evidence-based decisions.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A study group drills the six pillars as one sequence. Which order matches the way the framework lists them?
options: Cost Optimization
Governance
Operational Excellence
Sustainability
Performance Efficiency
Security
questions.explanation: The dossier lists the six pillars as Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability, so the keyed cards run 2, 5, 4, 0, 3, with Reliability simply not on the table. The card at index 1 is not a pillar at all: Governance is one of the six AWS CAF perspectives, which judge organizational readiness rather than workload quality. Listing order carries no priority, because the dossier states that no pillar wins automatically and no pillar has priority order, so the sequence is a recall aid and not a rule about satisfaction.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A reviewer sorts what each pillar delivers. Match each pillar to the value the framework attaches to it.
prompts: Operational Excellence
Security
Reliability
Performance Efficiency
Cost Optimization
Sustainability
options: Resilience
Right-sized spend
Agility and staff productivity
ESG performance
Resilience and compliance
Lower total cost of ownership
questions.explanation: The dossier's pillar-to-value map is Operational Excellence to agility and staff productivity, Security to resilience and compliance, Reliability to resilience, Performance Efficiency to right-sized spend, Cost Optimization to lower total cost of ownership, and Sustainability to ESG performance. The trap pair is Security against Reliability: both sound like resilience, so the card that adds compliance belongs to Security while plain resilience belongs to Reliability. Two further traps: right-sized spend belongs to Performance Efficiency rather than Cost Optimization, and ESG performance belongs to Sustainability even though cost and sustainability both talk about reduction.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 - Design principles of the AWS Cloud
questions.question: A coach checks sentences in her pillar notes before a workshop. Which sentences are accurate?
options: Security and Reliability both talk about resilience, so the stem's wording decides the pillar
Sustainability and Cost Optimization both talk about reduction, so the stem's wording decides the pillar
No pillar wins automatically and no pillar has a published priority order
Security is satisfied first in every review because it outranks the other pillars
Governance sits between Security and Reliability as a seventh pillar
Scalability is the pillar that absorbs growth so the other pillars need not change
questions.explanation: The dossier warns that similar words live in different pillars: Security and Reliability both talk about resilience, Sustainability and Cost Optimization both talk about reduction, and the stem's wording decides which list is live. It also states that no pillar wins automatically, no pillar has priority order, and the correct posture is a deliberate, measured trade-off, which is what Task 1.2 means by differences between the pillars. Option D asserts the priority the dossier denies. Option E mixes lists, because Governance is a CAF perspective and the Well-Architected set stops at six. Option F is the designed distractor: scalability is a Domain 1 cloud benefit, never one of the six pillars.

questions.question: A question asks: which is NOT one of the 6 Rs for migrating applications to the cloud?
options: Refactor
Relocate
Repurchase
Replatform
questions.explanation: The 6 Rs are Rehost, Replatform, Repurchase, Refactor, Retire and Retain. Relocate: the hypervisor-level lift and shift: was added when AWS moved to the 7 Rs in AWS Prescriptive Guidance. It is the designed bait for this exact stem.

questions.question: A regulated workload cannot change yet but must be reviewed again in eighteen months. Which migration strategy fits, and which list does it come from?
options: Retire, from the 6 Rs
Retain, from the 6 Rs (and the 7 Rs)
Relocate, from the 6 Rs
Replatform, from the 7 Rs
questions.explanation: Retain means 'keep it and revisit later': correct for a critical workload you cannot change now. Retain is in BOTH the 6 Rs (2016 blog) and the 7 Rs (current Prescriptive Guidance). Relocate is the 7 Rs-only strategy, so it cannot come from the 6 Rs; Retire means decommissioning, and Replatform implies an optimization you have just ruled out.

questions.question: The exam guide lists 'database replication' as an example of a migration strategy. Which service pair implements it?
options: AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces and AWS Transfer Family
AWS Snowball Edge and AWS Storage Gateway
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) for continuous replication and AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) for schema conversion
AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) and AWS DataSync
questions.explanation: Database replication is DMS (continuous replication while the application keeps running) plus SCT (schema and code conversion so the target accepts it). MGN is the rehost tool, not a database tool; Snowball is physical data transfer; Migration Hub Refactor Spaces and AWS Transfer Family are explicitly OUT OF SCOPE for this exam.

questions.question: Which list correctly names the six perspectives of the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF)?
options: Business, People, Culture, Platform, Security, Operations
Business, Process, People, Platform, Operations, Security
Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security, Operations
Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability
questions.explanation: AWS CAF groups its capabilities in six perspectives: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations. Option C is the Well-Architected pillar set. Option D is the six dimensions named by the MAP Assess phase: close, but 'process' is not a CAF perspective and 'Governance' is missing.

questions.question: A transformation office reports progress against the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework and the Migration Acceleration Program. Which statements are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: Process is one of the six AWS CAF perspectives
A CAF-led program targets reduced business risk
The MAP Assess phase lists Governance among its six dimensions
A CAF-led program targets improved environmental, social and governance performance
MAP credit amounts are published by AWS, so quote them in the business case
A CAF-led program targets increased revenue and increased operational efficiency
questions.explanation: The dossier names four examinable outcomes of a CAF-led program: reduced business risk; improved ESG performance; increased revenue; increased operational efficiency. Option A fails because the CAF perspectives are Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations: 'process' belongs to the six MAP Assess dimensions (business, process, people, platform, operations, security), which are explicitly NOT the CAF six. Option C fails for the mirror reason: Governance is missing from the MAP dimension list. Option E violates the dossier warning: AWS publishes only 'financial investments', so no MAP credit amount may ever be quoted.

questions.question: A logistics company planning a large offline data transfer has read three different AWS pages about AWS Snowball. Which statements are correct as of Oct 2026?
options: One Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device moves approximately 210 TB
Snowball Edge is currently available to every new AWS customer
A Snowball job must be completed within 360 days of being prepared
The device appears on this exam's current in-scope services list
AWS will discontinue support for Snowball in all AWS commercial Regions on 31 December 2026
The PDF exam guide still names use of AWS Snowball in Task 1.3
questions.explanation: The dossier's Snowball reality check states that one Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device moves approximately 210 TB (as of Oct 2026), that a job must be completed within 360 days of being prepared, that AWS will discontinue support for Snowball devices in all AWS commercial Regions on December 31, 2026 (GovCloud and ADC Region customers with active jobs unaffected, announcement as of Oct 2026), and that the PDF exam guide names 'use of AWS Snowball' in Task 1.3. Option B fails against the documentation banner that the device is no longer available to new customers. Option D fails because the device is on neither the in-scope nor the out-of-scope list, which makes it a trap in both directions rather than an in-scope answer.

questions.question: A program board wants the migration journey drawn in the order AWS publishes it. Which sequence is correct for the cards on the whiteboard?
options: Mobilize
Retire applications that are no longer useful
Assess
Migrate and Modernize
questions.explanation: The dossier gives the journey as Assess, then Mobilize, then Migrate and Modernize, because the gaps found in Assess have to be closed before migration starts, which is exactly why Mobilize sits between the business case and the first wave. The keyed sequence is therefore 2, 0, 3. The distractor at index 1 is a migration strategy (Retire, one of the 6 Rs), not a phase of the journey, so it belongs in a strategy conversation rather than on the journey timeline. Note also that the board's layout puts Mobilize first and Assess third: card position never overrides the published phase order.

questions.question: A consultancy maps its delivery teams onto AWS CAF perspectives before a migration engagement. Match each responsibility to the perspective that owns it.
prompts: Strategy, transformation and value realization
Culture, organization structure and workforce skills
Maximize benefits, minimize risk and portfolio management
Scalable hybrid platform, modernization and migration factory
Services delivered at agreed business levels
Confidentiality, integrity and availability
options: People
Security
Operations
Business
Governance
Platform
questions.explanation: The dossier pairs the six CAF perspectives with their typical owners: Business (CEO, CFO, COO, CIO, CTO: strategy, transformation, value realization), People (HR and culture leads), Governance (risk, finance, compliance), Platform (architects: scalable hybrid platform, modernization, migration factory), Security (CISO and security teams), Operations (IT operations: services delivered at agreed business levels). Two traps decide most misses: 'risk, finance, compliance' belongs to Governance rather than Security, and 'migration factory' belongs to Platform rather than Operations, because Platform owns the build-out machinery of the migration itself. The published capability counts (People 7, Governance 7, Platform 7, Security 9, Operations 9 as of Oct 2026) never substitute for ownership, and no Business-perspective count is published.

questions.question: A migration board is halfway through moving a large application portfolio and the estate is still unstable. The sponsor wants the rewrite-for-cloud-native work started immediately. Which instruction matches the sequencing rule AWS guidance gives?
options: Start the rewrites first, because the most complex applications return the largest savings
Rehost, replatform, relocate and retire first, and modernize only after the migration is stable
Retire every application that is no longer useful, then pause until the estate is re-procured
Freeze the migration until every application has a completed cloud-native redesign on paper
questions.explanation: The sequencing rule for large migrations in the dossier is to rehost, replatform, relocate and retire first, and to modernize only after the migration is stable: gaps found earlier must not be compounded by rewrites mid-flight. Option 0's complexity-first claim has no basis in that rule, because order is set by stability, not by potential savings. Option 3 contradicts the rule outright, since assessment feeds the plan rather than blocking the waves. Option 2 inflates Retire, which AWS's own order-of-magnitude guidance sizes at only 10% to 20% of an enterprise IT portfolio, and invents a procurement pause the rule never mentions.

questions.question: AWS's own customer page for Philip Morris International records that the initial aggressive lift-and-shift yielded suboptimal results. What did the company do next, and how must the figures be quoted?
options: It restarted with AWS Professional Services and a partner, migrating 400 applications in two years from August 2020, and the figures are customer-claimed and unaudited
It restarted with AWS Professional Services and a partner, migrating 400 applications in two years from August 2020, and AWS guarantees those savings for every customer
It paused migration work for twelve months so that AWS could redesign the estate, and the timeline is an AWS-published average
It completed the migration alone with no partner involved, and the case study is an audited financial statement
questions.explanation: The dossier's strategy-beats-speed case states that AWS's own Philip Morris International page records the initial aggressive lift-and-shift as yielding suboptimal results, and that the company migrated 400 applications in two years starting August 2020 using AWS Professional Services with a partner (IBM), Well-Architected reviews and Amazon RDS: customer-claimed, unaudited figures. Option 1 fails on the guarantee, because case-study numbers are customer-claimed and unaudited and an 'up to' ceiling is never a promise to the next customer. Option 2 invents a pause and an AWS-published average timeline that the dossier never gives, and option 3 denies the partner while upgrading an unaudited customer claim into an audited statement.

questions.question: Leadership wants a data-driven business case and a TCO model for a proposed data-center exit, before any migration work starts. Which resource does the lesson name for that job?
options: AWS Pricing Calculator, because it estimates the cost of resources that do not exist yet
Migration Hub Refactor Spaces, because it tracks the financial case for each refactor wave
AWS Prescriptive Guidance, because it publishes the time-tested strategies behind the 7 Rs
AWS Migration Evaluator, because it builds the data-driven business case and the TCO model
questions.explanation: The dossier lists Migration Evaluator as the resource for a data-driven business case and TCO model, and the 2026 update box (as of October 2026) moved it onto the in-scope list under Migration and Transfer. Option 1 is out of scope: Migration Hub Refactor Spaces sits on the out-of-scope services list, so it cannot be the key while an in-scope service fits. Option 0 is the true-but-irrelevant trap: estimating a run-rate for a workload that does not exist yet is the AWS Pricing Calculator's job, and a run-rate estimate is not the business case the stem asks for. Option 2 is also true of AWS Prescriptive Guidance, which is the source of the time-tested strategies and the 7 Rs, but it answers a strategy question rather than a TCO business case.

questions.question: A CAF lead is briefing executives on how the six perspectives are sized. Which statement about published capability counts is accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: People 7, Governance 7, Platform 7, Security 9 and Operations 9 capabilities, with no Business-perspective count published
Business 7, People 7, Governance 7, Platform 7, Security 9 and Operations 9, giving a published total of 46
Security and Operations carry the fewest capabilities at 7 each, because they were added most recently
AWS publishes a single total capability count across the six perspectives, refreshed at every re:Invent
questions.explanation: The dossier's published CAF capability counts (as of Oct 2026) are People 7, Governance 7, Platform 7, Security 9 and Operations 9, and AWS does not publish a Business-perspective count in the sources verified for the lesson, so no total should be memorized. Option 1 invents a Business count of 7 and then a published total, which is exactly the arithmetic the lesson warns against. Option 2 inverts the ranking: Security and Operations are the joint largest at 9 capabilities, not the smallest at 7. Option 3 asserts a published roll-up that does not exist, and a re:Invent date is not a source for these counts.

questions.question: A governance reviewer checks a migration plan against the glosses AWS gives each strategy. Which statements describe what the strategy actually changes?
options: Replatform makes a small optimization, such as moving a self-managed database to a managed service, while the application code stays untouched
Refactor rewrites the application to use cloud-native features and is the most complex and costly of the strategies
Retain decommissions the workload so that it stops incurring cost
Retire removes or decommissions a workload that is no longer useful
Repurchase lifts and shifts the existing application with no edits
Rehost replaces the workload with a vendor's hosted product
questions.explanation: The dossier glosses each strategy by what it changes: Replatform is lift and reshape, a small optimization such as a move to a managed database with the code untouched; Refactor re-architects for cloud-native features and is the most complex and costly; Retire means decommission or remove. Option 2 swaps Retain with Retire: Retain is revisit, meaning keep the workload where it is and come back later, so it never stops cost by removal. Option 4 gives Repurchase Rehost's gloss: Repurchase is drop and shop, usually a replacement with a SaaS product, whereas lifting an application unchanged is Rehost. Option 5 gives Rehost the Repurchase gloss in return, because Rehost moves the workload verbatim rather than replacing it with a vendor's offering.

questions.question: A team is about to lift an application unchanged onto AWS. Which sequence matches the order the lesson gives for the tooling around that move?
options: AWS Database Migration Service starts continuous replication of the source database
AWS Application Migration Service executes the rehost
AWS Application Discovery Service maps the application dependencies
The team chooses the migration strategy for the application
questions.explanation: The dossier puts discovery before choice: AWS Application Discovery Service maps dependencies before you choose an R, and rehost execution is AWS Application Migration Service (MGN). The keyed sequence is therefore 2, 3, 1. The card at index 0 is a true fact about a different strategy: AWS Database Migration Service is the guide's named database-replication example, replicating the source database continuously while the application keeps running, so it answers a database question rather than a lift-and-shift one (T7). Position of the cards on the page never decides rank.

questions.question: A transformation office matches each need to the resource AWS names for it on the migration journey. Match every need to the resource that delivers it.
prompts: Tools, training and financial investments, credits tied to tagging
Phases, modules, tasks and subtasks tracked in one place
Time-tested strategies and step-by-step guides, source of the 7 Rs
Hands-on delivery capacity supplied by AWS itself
Third-party delivery capacity through certified partners
Estimate the target run-rate before you move anything
options: Migration Hub Journeys
AWS Pricing Calculator
AWS Professional Services
Migration Acceleration Program
Partner Network and Migration Competency
AWS Prescriptive Guidance
questions.explanation: The dossier's journey resources pair off like this: the Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) provides tools, training and financial investments and its credits require tagging, summarized as no tags, no credits; Migration Hub Journeys tracks phases, modules, tasks and subtasks in one place; AWS Prescriptive Guidance supplies time-tested strategies and step-by-step guides and is the source of the 7 Rs; AWS Professional Services is hands-on delivery capacity from AWS; the AWS Partner Network with Migration Competency Partners is third-party delivery capacity; and the AWS Pricing Calculator estimates the target run-rate before you move anything. Two traps decide most misses: never quote a MAP credit amount, because AWS publishes only financial investments, and do not swap AWS's own delivery capacity for a partner's. Migration Hub Refactor Spaces and AWS Transfer Family are on the out-of-scope list, so neither belongs anywhere in this set.

questions.question: A migration office rehearses the worked example of a 40-application portfolio. Which allocations match the figures the lesson works through?
options: Retire 4 and Retain 6 applications
Rehost 16 and Replatform 8 applications
Repurchase 3 and Refactor 3, with Relocate at 0
Relocate 8, the largest share of the portfolio
Retain 16, because regulated workloads dominate the example
Rehost 4, matching the Retire count exactly
questions.explanation: The dossier's 40-application example sums to 40 as Retire 4, Retain 6, Rehost 16, Relocate 0, Repurchase 3, Replatform 8 and Refactor 3, and those shares follow AWS's order-of-magnitude guidance that as much as 10% to 20% of an enterprise IT portfolio is no longer useful and can be turned off. Option 3 reverses the example: Relocate is 0 here, and it is the hypervisor-level lift and shift that belongs to the 7 Rs framing. Option 4 inflates Retain to 16, which is in fact Rehost's count in the same table, and option 5 hands Rehost the Retire count, so neither pairing survives the arithmetic.

questions.question: A colleague refreshed their notes in 2024. Which statement is TRUE as of October 2026?
options: The Domain 4 support task still names Developer Support and Enterprise On-Ramp as the paid support options candidates must recognize
Every AWS account gets the legacy 12-month Free Tier with t2.micro, regardless of when the account was created
AWS Database Savings Plans replaced Compute and EC2 Instance Savings Plans, so the 'up to 72%' Savings Plans figure no longer applies
Accounts created on or after 2025-07-15 get a 6-month Free Tier plus up to USD 200 in credits, while accounts created before that date keep the legacy 12-month tier
questions.explanation: The Free Tier change took effect 2025-07-15: newer accounts get 6 months (or until credits run out) with a USD 100 sign-up credit plus up to USD 100 earned, on t3.micro/t3.small/t4g.micro/t4g.small/c7i-flex.large/m7i-flex.large; older accounts keep the legacy 12-month tier (AWS News Blog, 2025-07-15; EC2 User Guide 'before and after July 15, 2025'). Option A is stale: the current guide's Task 4.3 names Basic Support, AWS Business Support+, AWS Enterprise Support and AWS Unified Operations (classic Developer/Business/Enterprise On-Ramp closed to new subscriptions after 2025-12-02). Option C is false: Database Savings Plans (launched 2025-12-02, up to 35% on a 1-year commitment) are an addition, not a replacement. Free Tier and support-plan behaviour is date-stamped: verify current before use.

questions.question: AWS's Box case study is titled 'Unpacks over 2.23 USD Million in Savings'. Which breakdown of that total matches the AWS publication (figures as published, accessed Oct 2026)?
options: 438,000 USD from rightsizing + 1.1 USD million from storage tiering + 500,000 USD from egress + 192,000 USD from logging
1,100,000 USD from inter-AZ transfer + 500,000 USD from egress + 438,000 USD from storage + 192,000 USD from logging
438,000 USD inter-AZ transfer + 1.1 USD million per year internet egress + over 500,000 USD per year storage + 192,000 USD per year logging
2,230,000 USD from a single Spot-instance commitment that covers all four categories at once
questions.explanation: AWS publishes Box's 2.23 USD million as four separate billing concepts: 438,000 USD of inter-AZ data transfer, 1.1 USD million per year of internet egress, over 500,000 USD per year of storage (S3/S3 Glacier tiering), and 192,000 USD per year of logging (AWS case study, accessed Oct 2026). The distractors scramble the pairs, and Option D is wrong twice over: Box's savings came from a Well-Architected review and architecture fixes: the free lever: not from an interruptible-capacity purchase, and no single mechanism produced the total. As with every case study, these are customer-claimed, unaudited figures, never an AWS guarantee.

questions.question: Canva's AWS-published cost case study (accessed Oct 2026) reports compute costs down 46% in under two years after the company split its workloads across three purchase options: Spot for interruptible free-tier projects, On-Demand plus Savings Plans for steady Pro-user capacity, and Reserved Instances as a fallback. Why is that mix the correct design?
options: Because Reserved Instances commit to a dollar amount per hour while Savings Plans commit to a specific configuration
Because Savings Plans are always the cheapest option, so any workload not covered by one is automatically overpaying
Because buying a Savings Plan removes Spot interruption risk whenever both are purchased for the same workload

Because each option answers a different constraint: Spot buys interruptible capacity at up to 90% off with a two-minute notice, a Savings Plan discounts a steady USD per hour commitment, and On-Demand keeps unmatched spiky capacity flexible
questions.explanation: Spot's ceiling: up to 90% off: fits only fault-tolerant, checkpointable work, a Savings Plan commits to usage measured in USD per hour and auto-applies without an exchange, and On-Demand remains the flexible remainder. The second option is wrong because commitment discounts are not cheapest for unpredictable or interruptible work; the third is wrong because Spot usage is explicitly excluded from Savings Plans; the fourth reverses the definitions: a Savings Plan commits to USD per hour, a Reserved Instance commits to a configuration (Standard up to 72%, Convertible up to 66% as of Oct 2026).

questions.question: Using the illustrative TCO table in this lesson (on-premises 233,500 USD vs AWS 117,000 USD over five years, migration investment 25,000 USD: teaching figures, as of Oct 2026, not AWS list prices), what are the five-year ROI and the simple payback period?
options: ROI 366%; payback about 5 years
ROI 49.9%; payback about 5 years
ROI 49.9%; payback about 13 months
ROI 366%; payback about 13 months
questions.explanation: Net benefit = 116,500 USD - 25,000 USD = 91,500 USD; ROI = 91,500 / 25,000 x 100 = 366%. Average annual saving = 116,500 / 5 = 23,300 USD; payback = 25,000 / 23,300 = 1.07 years, about 13 months. The 49.9% figure is the TCO reduction percentage (116,500 / 233,500), not the ROI: the exam deliberately confuses the two.

questions.question: A finance team builds a five-year cost model before approving an on-premises refresh. Which inputs does Task 1.4 require the model to include?
options: Only the server purchase price compared against an hourly cloud rate
Hardware and annual maintenance contracts
Nothing beyond depreciation, because facilities belong to the landlord
Operating system, hypervisor and application licences
Space, power and cooling, plus IT labour
The five-year refresh cycle and the cost of capital
questions.explanation: Task 1.4's named on-premises cost drivers are hardware, annual maintenance, operating system and hypervisor licences, application licences (often the largest single line), space, power and cooling, IT labour, the five-year refresh cycle, six to nine months procurement lead time, 20% to 50% over-provisioning, cost of capital and bandwidth. Option A is the flawed comparison the dossier says AWS warns about: the hidden-inputs example reaches a 193,500 USD subtotal before software licences, the year-5 refresh, cost of capital and bandwidth (illustrative teaching figures, as of Oct 2026, not AWS list prices). Option C fails because space, power and cooling is a named driver, so a model that hands it to the landlord understates the estate.

questions.question: A cost team drafts the runbook it will follow before renewing any commitment. Which sequence matches the order AWS's FinOps guidance gives for the levers shown?
options: Move fault-tolerant batch work to interruptible capacity
Commit to a discount before measuring utilisation
Rightsize against measured utilisation
Add a commitment discount for steady baseline usage
Freeze the current instance shapes so the discount applies cleanly
questions.explanation: The dossier gives the canonical FinOps ordering as rightsizing first, then commitment, then interruptible capacity, because committing to a discount on an oversized instance buys a discount on waste. The keyed sequence is therefore 2, 3, 0. Option 1 commits before measuring, which reverses the order of operations: rightsizing matches instance size and type to measured utilisation while still meeting performance requirements, and only then does a commitment make sense. Option 4 freezes the estate in place, which is the opposite of rightsizing and matches no published step. The table layout puts the last lever at the top, so position on the page never decides rank.

questions.question: A regulated company is deciding how to run licensed software on AWS. Match each need to the option or tool AWS names for it.
prompts: You own the licence and the media, and you own compliance
Licence cost is bundled into the instance price while it runs
Rightsizing recommendations plus idle-resource identification
Licence position tracked across AWS, on-premises and other clouds
options: AWS License Manager
License-included pricing
AWS Compute Optimizer
Bring your own licence
questions.explanation: The dossier separates the licensing choices cleanly: with BYOL you bring the licence and the media, you own compliance, and the marginal licence cost is about zero; with license-included pricing the licence is bundled into the instance price, AWS owns licensing compliance, and you pay only while the instance runs. AWS License Manager is the free in-scope tool that tracks licences across AWS, on-premises and other clouds, while AWS Compute Optimizer provides rightsizing recommendations and identifies idle resources. The trap is responsibility flipping in either direction: compliance never moves to AWS when you bring your own licence, and AWS never audits an estate you do not report into License Manager. The illustrative break-even in the dossier (a 150 USD per month licence divided by 0.75 - 0.40 USD per hour, about 428.6 hours or roughly 59 percent uptime, teaching figures as of Oct 2026) only decides which pricing option wins on cost.

questions.question: A Windows workload runs only 30% of the month. Which licensing strategy and ordering rule does AWS guidance support?
options: BYOL, because an existing licence always beats paying for one: and rightsizing should be done after choosing a commitment model
License-included, because you pay for the bundled licence only while the instance runs: and rightsizing should be done BEFORE choosing a discount or commitment model
Either, because licensing has no effect on cloud economics
License-included, and auto scaling should be applied before any rightsizing
questions.explanation: At 30% uptime the license-included option wins because AWS bundles the licence and you pay only while running (and AWS owns licensing compliance); BYOL wins only above roughly 59% uptime in our illustrative model. The canonical FinOps order is rightsizing first: match measured utilization: then choose a commitment/discount such as Savings Plans, because committing to a discount on an oversized instance buys a discount on waste.

questions.question: A test environment is switched off for a whole quarter while an on-premises rack stays powered. Which pair of figures from the lesson's twelve-month example fits this situation?
options: The on-premises row falls to 0 USD for that quarter while the cloud row stays flat at 6,000 USD per quarter
Both rows fall to 0 USD, because depreciation stops as soon as the workload stops
The cloud row falls to 0 USD for that quarter while the on-premises row stays flat at 6,000 USD per quarter
The cloud row stays at 3,900 USD, because metered resources are billed for a full quarter once reserved
questions.explanation: The dossier's twelve-month example (illustrative teaching figures, as of Oct 2026, not AWS list prices) keeps on-premises flat at 6,000 USD per quarter, that is 24,000 USD for the year, while the AWS rows read 4,200 + 2,700 + 1,350 + 3,900 = 12,150 USD, a difference of 11,850 USD or -49.4%; the cloud row can drop to zero for a workload switched off, and the test environment reads 0 USD in Q3. That is the mechanic: fixed cost exists whether or not the service runs, variable cost tracks consumption. Option 0 reverses the two rows (T5), option 1 is wrong because depreciation of owned hardware continues whether the workload runs or not, and option 3 attaches a real figure from Q4 to a reservation rule the meter does not have (T6).

questions.question: A finance lead asks how moving to the cloud changes the accounting classification of infrastructure spend. Which statement matches the lesson?
options: Cloud spend becomes capex whenever an instance runs for more than a year, and opex otherwise
On-premises spend is opex because utilities and rent are paid monthly, while cloud spend is capex because you commit to a configuration
Capex turns into variable cost the moment the hardware is installed, so the two terms are interchangeable
On-premises spend is capex: it buys an asset you own and depreciate over about a five-year cycle; cloud spend is opex: it is expensed in the period it is incurred
questions.explanation: The dossier states the accounting fact directly: capex buys an asset you own and depreciate over about a five-year cycle, opex is expensed in the period it is incurred, and the cloud turns capex into opex, which is the first of the six advantages restated. Option 0 is the designed reversal (T5): the dossier warns that a distractor will flip the direction, because on-premises is capex and fixed while the cloud is opex and variable. Option 2 collapses capex into variable cost, but the two definitions never meet: fixed cost exists whether or not the service runs, whereas variable cost tracks consumption. Option 3 invents a duration rule the lesson never states, so a commitment or a long-running instance does not reclassify the spend.

questions.question: A stakeholder dismisses total cost of ownership as the price list for the cloud over five years. Which correction matches what the lesson says TCO actually is?
options: TCO is the price list AWS publishes for every service, refreshed whenever a price changes
TCO counts only what you acquire, because operating costs are reported separately as ROI
TCO is the all-in, multi-year comparison of acquisition AND operating costs: hardware, software, facilities, labour and capital
TCO covers a single year, because anything beyond twelve months is a forecast rather than a cost
questions.explanation: The dossier defines TCO as the all-in, multi-year comparison of acquisition AND operating costs: hardware, software, facilities, labour and capital, and says explicitly that it is not a price list. Option 0 restates the stakeholder's own error, so it cannot be the correction. Option 1 mixes two different measures: operating costs belong inside TCO, while ROI compares net benefit against the investment made to earn it, which is why the exam delights in pairing a TCO reduction with an ROI figure. Option 3 contradicts the five-year horizon the comparison requires, because acquisition costs such as the hardware refresh only make sense across the multi-year window.

questions.question: An operations lead argues that automation on AWS is a technical convenience rather than an economic lever. Which statements support the economic case the lesson makes?
options: Infrastructure as code means provisioning and supporting infrastructure using code instead of manual processes and settings
AWS CloudFormation templates are versioned, reviewable, repeatable and rollback-able
Fewer undifferentiated tasks mean less staff time and less software to license
Automation is the same thing as auto scaling, so it only matters when demand spikes
Amazon DynamoDB still leaves capacity management and operational overhead with the customer
Automation guarantees the lowest possible bill regardless of how the workload is used
questions.explanation: Task 1.4's benefits of automation are economic: infrastructure as code replaces manual processes and settings, the guide's named example is AWS CloudFormation whose templates are versioned, reviewable, repeatable and rollback-able, and managed services absorb undifferentiated work, so fewer undifferentiated tasks mean less staff time and less software to license. Option 3 is the classic confusion: automation is not auto scaling, because CloudFormation makes provisioning repeatable while Auto Scaling provides elasticity. Option 4 flips a responsibility the dossier assigns to AWS: Amazon DynamoDB takes capacity management and operational overhead off the customer. Option 5 is an over-claim (T4): no automation guarantees a bill, and utilisation still has to be measured before anything is resized or committed.

questions.question: A CFO asks for the life story of an on-premises server rack in the order it happens. Which sequence matches the cost drivers Task 1.4 names?
options: Annual maintenance renewals replace the hardware every year
The asset is depreciated over roughly a five-year cycle
Six to nine months of procurement lead time pass before delivery
The fleet is deployed 20% to 50% above peak-predicted demand
The five-year refresh cycle replaces the fleet
questions.explanation: Task 1.4's on-premises drivers play out in this order: six to nine months of procurement lead time pass before the hardware arrives, the fleet is then deployed 20% to 50% above peak-predicted demand, the asset is depreciated across roughly a five-year cycle, and the five-year refresh replaces it. The keyed sequence is therefore 2, 3, 1, 4. The card at index 0 is the numeric bait (T6): annual maintenance is a real yearly line in the model, but renewals never replace hardware, the five-year refresh does. A cost model that drops either the maintenance line or the refresh understates the estate.

questions.question: An analyst rebuilds the hidden-inputs example for ten servers over five years. Match each figure to the line it totals.
options: Subtotal reached before licences, refresh, capital and bandwidth
Power and cooling: 25 USD x 10 servers x 60 months
Hardware purchase, and equally the annual maintenance total
Floor space for the ten servers across five years
Administration labour at 0.25 full-time equivalent
questions.explanation: The dossier's hidden-inputs example totals 30,000 USD hardware plus 30,000 USD maintenance plus 15,000 USD power and cooling (25 USD x 10 servers x 60 months) plus 6,000 USD floor space plus 112,500 USD for 0.25 FTE of administration, giving a 193,500 USD subtotal that sits BEFORE software licences, the year-5 refresh, cost of capital and bandwidth (illustrative teaching figures, as of Oct 2026, not AWS list prices). Two traps decide the misses: hardware and annual maintenance happen to carry the same five-year figure, so 30,000 USD matches both lines rather than only the purchase price, and 193,500 USD is not the finished comparison, because the flawed model AWS warns about is the one that stops at the server purchase price against an hourly cloud rate.

questions.question: A new team member summarizes the AWS shared responsibility model as follows. Which statement is correct?
options: AWS is responsible for security in the cloud, and the customer is responsible for security of the cloud
AWS is responsible for security of the cloud, and the customer is responsible for security in the cloud
AWS and the customer split security equally, 50/50, regardless of the services used
The customer is responsible for security of the cloud only when using Amazon EC2
questions.explanation: AWS's own wording is security OF the cloud (protecting the infrastructure that runs all AWS services) versus security IN the cloud (the customer's duties, determined by the services selected). The prepositions are fixed, the split is never 50/50: shared controls apply in completely separate contexts: and the customer side exists on every service, not just EC2.

questions.question: A security reviewer claims AWS configures the security group firewall for an Amazon EC2 instance because AWS provides it. What does the shared responsibility model actually say?
options: Correct - AWS provides and configures all firewall components for every service
Correct: security groups are an inherited control because the firewall is AWS hardware
Incorrect: the customer is responsible for the configuration of the AWS-provided security group firewall
Incorrect: security groups are configured by AWS Support on the customer's behalf
questions.explanation: AWS's canonical text names it directly: the customer assumes responsibility for the guest OS, associated application software, and the configuration of the AWS provided security group firewall. Providing a capability is not the same as configuring it: the configuration is customer responsibility, which makes security group rules a customer-specific control.

questions.question: A team moves a legacy Oracle database to Amazon RDS Custom because it needs privileged operating-system access. What happens to patching responsibility?
options: AWS still patches the guest OS and the database engine, exactly as with standard Amazon RDS
The customer manages the host and customizes the OS as in Amazon EC2, so OS patching and database software patching return to the customer
Neither party patches it: RDS Custom runs without patches by design
AWS patches the OS only, while a third-party partner patches the database engine
questions.explanation: AWS documents RDS Custom as using managed RDS features while the customer manages the host and customizes the OS as in Amazon EC2: and its responsibility table flips OS patching and DB software patching to Customer. That makes 'Amazon RDS means AWS patches everything' a false absolute, which is exactly why RDS Custom appears as a distractor.

questions.question: An Amazon EC2 instance runs a customer application and needs a security patch for its guest operating system. Who is responsible for applying it?
options: AWS, because AWS owns the infrastructure beneath the instance
The customer, because the guest operating system (including updates and security patches) is customer responsibility
AWS, because patch management is listed as an AWS-only control
The customer only if the instance is in a single-tenant Availability Zone
questions.explanation: AWS operates and controls components from the host operating system and virtualization layer downward; the customer assumes responsibility for the guest operating system including updates and security patches. Patch management is a SHARED control in separate contexts: AWS fixes flaws in its infrastructure, you fix your guest OS: and Availability Zone tenancy is irrelevant to the boundary.

questions.question: The CLF-C02 exam guide says AWS and customer responsibilities can shift depending on the service used. Which responsibility shifts across Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS and AWS Lambda?
options: Who owns customer data, which is always the customer
Who configures IAM permissions, which is always the customer
Who performs guest OS and runtime patching, which is the customer on EC2, AWS on standard Amazon RDS, and AWS (with customer-triggered updates in some Lambda modes) for Lambda
Who physically secures the data centre, which moves to the customer on serverless services
questions.explanation: Task 2.1 explicitly names EC2, RDS and Lambda as shift examples, and what moves is the infrastructure duty: guest OS patching and engine patching. Data ownership, IAM configuration and physical security are fixed anchors: data, IAM and facilities never move across the line.
