questions.question: After a regional outage review, a resilience lead splits a slide into guarantees on one side and duties on the other. Which entries belong to resiliency OF the cloud, the half AWS commits to itself?
options: Service availability that meets or exceeds AWS Service Level Agreements
At least three physically separate Availability Zones engineered into every Region
An N+1 power and cooling standard inside every AWS data centre
A multi-AZ database topology that your own team switches on
Quarterly failover tests scheduled and executed by your engineers
Backup, versioning and replication settings chosen on your storage
questions.explanation: The dossier's resiliency OF the cloud is infrastructure availability meeting or exceeding AWS Service Level Agreements, with at least three physically separate Availability Zones per Region and an N+1 data-centre standard, all engineered by AWS. The three distractors are resiliency IN the cloud: AWS never designs your multi-AZ topology, schedules your failover tests, or picks your backup, versioning and replication settings, because that half is described as customers designing, testing and deploying their own applications.

questions.question: A vendor pitch claims managed services absorb every operational chore. The architecture review strikes parts of that list. Which duties still sit with your engineers on every service you run?
options: Classifying the data your application stores before it is uploaded
Deciding whether stored data is encrypted, and which key type to use
Granting least-privilege permissions to an IAM role
Patching the hypervisor that sits beneath your instances
Applying engine patches to a standard Amazon RDS database
Sanitizing retired media that held customer data, under NIST 800-88
questions.explanation: The dossier lists six duties that never move off the customer: data classification, identity and access management, OS patching on customer-run layers, network configuration, encryption choices and application security. So classifying stored data, choosing the encryption and key type, and granting permissions stay yours on every service. The distractors are AWS-side infrastructure: AWS owns the hypervisor under your instances, patches the host OS and database engine on standard Amazon RDS, and decommissions media under NIST 800-88 as an inherited physical control.

questions.question: A security operations lead is standing up a fresh account and writes the recurring monitoring checklist for that account. Put these steps in the order the team actually performs them.
options: Review the findings your monitoring tools have collected
Remediate: rotate keys, tighten rules, patch, close public exposure
Enable the AWS monitoring tools for this account
Evidence the work: retain the logs and export reports for auditors
AWS supplies the monitoring tools the program will call on
Wait for AWS Support to remediate each finding on your behalf
questions.explanation: The dossier's customer-side loop runs AWS supplies the tools, then the CUSTOMER enables them, reviews findings, remediates by rotating, tightening, patching and closing exposure, and finally evidences the work with retained logs and exported reports, before gaps feed back into the next enablement pass. That gives supply, enable, review, remediate, evidence. The decoy fails because the loop is entirely customer-run once the tools exist: findings you never collect are findings nobody remediates, and AWS Support is not a remediation service.

questions.question: A new engineer sketches the responsibility boundary as stacked layers. Reading from the top of the customer's side down to AWS, what is the correct sequence of these four layers?
options: Physical facility: power, cooling and floor security
Guest operating system: updates and security patches
Application software your developers write and run
Host operating system and virtualization layer
questions.explanation: The dossier's canonical sentence gives AWS everything from the host operating system and virtualization layer down to physical security, while the customer takes the guest OS, associated application software and configuration above that line; in stack form layers 3 to 7 are yours and the lower layers are AWS's. Reading top-down therefore gives application software, then guest OS, then host OS plus virtualization layer, then the facility. Placing the facility or the hypervisor on the customer's side reverses the boundary.

questions.question: Match each control below to the category AWS's own definitions place it in: inherited, shared in separate contexts, or customer specific:
prompts: Badge readers, guards and cameras at the facility
Patch management carried out on both sides of the line
Configuration management applied by both parties
Awareness and training programs for the workforce
Data classification, IAM and encryption decisions
options: Shared: patch management, separate contexts
Inherited: fully from AWS, no customer work
Shared: configuration management, separate contexts
Customer specific: data, IAM and encryption choices
Shared: awareness and training, separate contexts
questions.explanation: The dossier gives the official wording: inherited controls are those a customer fully inherits from AWS, with physical and environmental controls such as badges, guards, cameras, power and cooling as the canonical example. Shared controls apply to both layers but in completely separate contexts, and there are exactly three: patch management, configuration management, and awareness and training. Customer specific controls cover service and communications protection plus data classification, IAM and encryption decisions, which is why the last prompt lands there rather than on a shared control.

questions.question: A Lambda function uses a runtime pinned to an older version and the function is configured for Manual runtime updates. AWS has already published a security fix for that runtime. Who must act?
options: AWS, because Lambda is responsible for all runtime security regardless of update mode
AWS Support, when the customer opens a ticket about the deprecated runtime
The customer: for functions configured to use the Manual runtime update mode, the customer is responsible for updating the function to the latest runtime version
Neither - Lambda runtimes never receive security updates
questions.explanation: AWS curates and publishes security updates for supported managed runtimes and container images, but in Manual mode the responsibility to update the function sits with the customer. In Auto mode Lambda applies updates to all functions, and for container images AWS publishes patched base images that you must rebuild: the service class alone never decides the answer.

questions.question: An operations team argues that because AWS guarantees infrastructure availability, its application does not need multi-AZ deployment or tested backups. Which response matches the model?
options: Correct - AWS SLAs cover the customer application end to end
Correct: resiliency is a shared control, so a 50/50 split means AWS handles the design

Incorrect - AWS is responsible for resiliency of the infrastructure against its SLAs, while the customer is responsible for designing, testing and deploying the application, including multi-AZ design and backups
Incorrect: the customer is responsible for resiliency of the cloud infrastructure as well
questions.explanation: The resiliency axis mirrors the security axis: resiliency OF the cloud (infrastructure availability meeting or exceeding AWS SLAs) is AWS; resiliency IN the cloud (Multi-AZ design, backups, replication, DR testing) is the customer. SLA coverage of the infrastructure never extends to how you deploy on top of it, and resiliency is not a 50/50 control.

questions.question: Under the shared responsibility model, a team moves a workload from on-premises to Amazon EC2 and then to Amazon RDS. Which task moves to AWS at the RDS step but NOT at the EC2 step?
options: Operating system patching and database software patching
Configuring the AWS-provided firewall called a security group
Application optimization and query tuning
Managing customer data and choosing IAM permissions
questions.explanation: The published matrix shows OS patching and database patching as Customer on premises and on EC2, and as AWS on RDS: that is exactly the shift the RDS step buys you. Server maintenance, hardware lifecycle and power/cooling move to AWS already at the EC2 step. Security group configuration, application optimization, data and IAM stay with the customer everywhere.

questions.question: A design review records the claim that shared responsibility divides every control between AWS and the customer. Which correction matches AWS's own definition of the model?
options: Shared means two different organizations, each fully responsible for its own layer, with the boundary moving according to the service selected
Shared means every control is split evenly, so AWS and the customer each complete half of the same control
Shared means the customer can hand half of its controls to AWS by accepting an agreement in AWS Artifact
Shared means AWS covers every control until the customer passes a free usage tier, after which the customer owns it
questions.explanation: AWS's premise is that two different organizations are each fully responsible for its own layer, and the boundary between those layers moves depending on which service you pick (2.1, the shared responsibility premise). Option 1 is the sentence the model explicitly rejects: shared controls apply to both layers but in completely separate contexts, so nothing is ever split evenly. Option 2 mistakes inheritance for delegation, because AWS Artifact holds AWS's own reports and agreements and inheritance shrinks the evidence you produce without transferring the obligation. Option 3 invents a usage-based boundary that appears nowhere in the model.

questions.question: A manager argues that because AWS provides CloudTrail and AWS Config, the audit evidence already exists in every account without any customer action. Which response matches the model?
options: Incorrect: both services run only on AWS-owned accounts and customers cannot enable them at all
Incorrect: providing a tool is not configuring it, so the customer enables these services in its own account and reviews what they collect
Correct: AWS turns both services on in every account and keeps the evidence on the customer's behalf
Correct: AWS ships the compliance evidence to the customer's auditor every quarter as part of the subscription
questions.explanation: The dossier's misattribution traps are provided is not configured and tool is not duty: AWS provides CloudTrail, AWS Config, KMS and the security group, while the customer configures, enables and acts, and the customer enables CloudTrail and Config for its own account (2.1, classic misattribution traps). Option 1 repeats the same flip as a promise, and option 3 is false because both services are enabled by customers in any account. Nothing in the model delivers finished evidence; findings you never collect are findings nobody remediates.

questions.question: A network engineer writes the responsibility matrix for a VPC estate. Which lines belong to your team, whichever AWS services the workloads run on?
options: Writing the security group rules that filter traffic to each network interface
Writing the numbered network ACL rules that apply at the subnet level
Designing the VPC layout: subnets, route tables and internet gateway attachment
Deciding whether a bucket is reachable from the internet through Block Public Access and the bucket policy
Replacing the failed network hardware inside the Availability Zone that hosts your subnets
Choosing the physical cabling between the data centre halls that serve the Region
questions.explanation: Network configuration is one of the six duties that never move off the customer: security group and NACL rules, VPC design, route tables, and whether a bucket is public (2.1, the six duties that never move). The responsibility matrix agrees, putting the AWS-provided firewall, the security group on the database endpoint, VPC configuration for a function and Block Public Access with the customer (2.1, responsibility shifts by service). Options 4 and 5 sit in security OF the cloud: AWS owns the hardware, networking and physical facilities from the host OS and virtualization layer downward, so no customer ever cables or swaps that gear.

questions.question: A platform team compares managed services on how much patch coordination it must plan for. Which statements are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: Single-tenant services such as Amazon RDS and Amazon OpenSearch Service are patched by AWS within the service's patching SLA
For those single-tenant services the customer selects maintenance windows and schedules any required restarts
Multi-tenant services such as Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3 are patched by AWS with no customer action required
For multi-tenant services the customer only consults the maintenance documentation
The customer applies operating system patches to a multi-tenant service as soon as AWS publishes them
AWS holds every single-tenant patch until the customer approves each one individually
questions.explanation: The dossier separates the two service shapes: single-tenant managed services are patched by AWS within the service's patching SLA while the customer facilitates by selecting maintenance windows, applying service updates and scheduling required restarts, and multi-tenant services are patched by AWS with no customer action beyond reading the maintenance documentation (2.1, single-tenant versus multi-tenant patching). Option 4 fails because a multi-tenant service exposes no guest operating system for you to patch, and option 5 inverts the SLA: AWS applies the patch inside it, and your role is coordinating the window, not approving the fix.

questions.question: Ranked from the service at which your team keeps the MOST infrastructure duties to the one at which it keeps the FEWEST, which sequence is correct?
options: AWS Lambda running your function code
Amazon S3 storing your objects
Amazon EC2 instances with a guest operating system you patch
Amazon RDS managed database deployment
questions.explanation: The published ladder reads Amazon EC2 (IaaS) to Amazon RDS (managed database) to AWS Lambda (serverless compute) to Amazon S3 (abstracted storage), because the line slides up as abstraction rises while your data, IAM, network configuration and encryption choice never move down the ladder (2.1, ordering of customer infrastructure duties). S3 first or Lambda first both invert the ladder: the guest OS and the database engine are duties you keep on EC2 and lose at RDS, and by Lambda there is no operating system left on your side at all.

questions.question: An assessor asks where your compliance evidence comes from. Put these steps in order, starting with AWS's own audit.
options: Your team downloads AWS's compliance reports from a self-service portal at no cost
AWS issues a certificate that covers your workload as soon as the reports are downloaded
Your team implements and evidences the controls that AWS does not cover
AWS is audited against its own control requirements throughout the year
Your team obtains the authorization for its workload from the body that issues it
AWS publishes its compliance reports for on-demand download by customers
questions.explanation: The chain in the dossier is: AWS is audited against more than 2,600 requirements throughout the year, AWS publishes those reports as on-demand downloads in a no-cost self-service portal, your team pulls them for its own evidence file, your team still implements and evidences the controls that remain yours, and your team holds the authorization (2.1, inheritance and AWS's own evidence; 2.2, AWS Artifact). Option 1 is the trap stated outright: no formal certification is available to (or distributable by) a cloud service provider, and AWS customers remain responsible for complying with applicable compliance laws and regulations, so nothing AWS downloads certifies your workload.

questions.question: Match each workload to the party responsible for patching the operating system or runtime it runs on:
prompts: An Amazon EC2 instance running a Linux guest OS you installed
A standard Amazon RDS database deployment
An Amazon RDS Custom deployment that needs host access
An AWS Lambda function on Auto runtime updates
Objects stored in an Amazon S3 bucket
options: AWS: abstracted storage, so no guest OS exists on your side
AWS: the OS and engine are patched, you choose the window
Customer: the guest OS and its security patches are yours
AWS: Lambda applies runtime updates to every function
Customer: you manage the host and customize the OS
questions.explanation: The workload-to-patcher table keys each row by what the service exposes: on Amazon EC2 the guest OS and its security patches are yours, standard Amazon RDS keeps OS and engine patching with AWS while you only pick the maintenance window, Amazon RDS Custom flips both back to you because you manage the host and customize the OS as in Amazon EC2, Lambda in Auto mode has the service apply runtime updates to all functions, and Amazon S3 is abstracted multi-tenant storage with no guest OS on your side (2.1, workload to who patches the OS or runtime). The two traps are reading a managed label as AWS does everything, and forgetting that the RDS Custom escape hatch returns OS and database patching to the customer.

questions.question: A company wants to stop member accounts from launching resources outside two approved Regions, without granting any new permissions. The organization uses the all-features set. What should you do?
options: Attach a deny-only Service Control Policy at the relevant OU or the root
Attach an SCP that allows only the two approved Regions, because SCPs grant permissions
Attach an IAM policy to every user in every member account
Move the accounts into a new OU, because OU membership itself blocks Region launches
questions.explanation: SCPs are a deny-only ceiling: AWS says 'SCPs do not grant permissions', effective permissions are the intersection with IAM, and any Deny anywhere wins. An SCP that says 'allow' changes nothing on its own. OU structure alone never restricts anything, and per-user IAM policies do not give organization-wide governance. Note also that SCPs have no effect on the management account.

questions.question: A healthcare startup asks whether AWS is HIPAA certified and what it must do to process protected health information. Which response is correct?
options: No cloud service provider can hold a HIPAA certification; AWS will sign a standard BAA that you accept in AWS Artifact, you may use only HIPAA-eligible services for PHI, and you remain responsible for your share of compliance
Yes: the HIPAA certificate is downloadable from AWS Config conformance packs
Yes - AWS holds a HIPAA certification in every Region, so no further action is needed once you select a Region
No - HIPAA applies only to on-premises systems, so the question does not arise on AWS
questions.explanation: AWS states explicitly: 'There is no HIPAA certification for a cloud service provider (CSP) such as AWS.' AWS aligns with HHS rules, will sign a standard BAA accepted in AWS Artifact, and only HIPAA-eligible services may process PHI: while the customer keeps its own obligations. Conformance packs are AWS Config artifacts, not certification stores.

questions.question: A regulated workload must ensure customer data is never stored or processed outside eu-central-1. Which combination BEST enforces this?
options: Enable eu-central-1 and rely on engineers to select it, then monitor with CloudWatch alarms on data transfer
Download the residency statement from AWS Artifact and file it with the auditor
A weekly AWS Trusted Advisor refresh plus a conformance pack in the management account
Control Tower data-residency guardrails (preventive controls delivered as SCPs), the workload isolated in its own account or OU, and cross-Region networking restricted
questions.explanation: AWS states that AWS Control Tower provides governance and controls for data residency, and its residency guardrails are preventive controls whose artifact is an SCP: so a Region-leaving action is denied and logged in CloudTrail. Isolating the workload and restricting cross-Region networking complete the control. CloudWatch monitors, Trusted Advisor advises, and Artifact only holds AWS's own documents.

questions.question: Which statement about AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) is correct?
options: An SCP attached to an OU grants the permissions it lists to every IAM role in the accounts beneath it
SCPs replace IAM entirely, so member-account identity policies become redundant
SCPs apply only to the management account, because member accounts keep their own policies
An SCP sets the maximum available permissions: it never grants, an explicit deny at any level wins, and it does not affect users or roles in the management account
questions.explanation: AWS states that SCPs provide central control over the maximum available permissions and that no permissions are granted by an SCP: effective permissions are the intersection with identity and resource policies, and a Deny at any level wins. SCPs do not affect users or roles in the management account (only member accounts, including their root user), and IAM remains the layer that actually grants access.

questions.question: You need AWS's SOC 2 report, its ISO 27001 certificate and a PCI Attestation of Compliance, and you must sign a Business Associate Agreement for your account and 20 member accounts. Where do you go?
options: AWS Artifact: free, self-service on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents plus agreements
AWS Trusted Advisor: the Security category publishes attestations
AWS Config: conformance packs export the reports
AWS Organizations: consolidated billing includes the agreements
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact provides on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents (ISO, PCI, SOC reports and certifications from accreditation bodies) free of charge, and it is where you review, accept and track agreements such as the BAA and NDA across accounts in your organization. Trusted Advisor advises, Config evaluates your resources, and Organizations handles structure and billing.

questions.question: A platform team on the Basic support plan drafts an internal memo about AWS Trusted Advisor. Which sentences in that memo survive a fact check as of Oct 2026?
options: The check categories are cost, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits and operational excellence
It only advises, because enforcement comes from Config rules, SCPs and Control Tower guardrails
Basic and Developer plans get console access with manual refresh plus a named subset of checks
Compliance is the seventh check category added for regulated workloads
It remediates each failed check automatically without any action from you
Every plan includes API and CLI access with weekly automatic refresh
questions.explanation: The dossier states Trusted Advisor has exactly six check categories, cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits and operational excellence, so an invented seventh compliance category is false; the service is advisory only, with enforcement coming from Config rules and remediation, SCPs and Control Tower guardrails; and depth is gated by plan, with Basic and Developer getting console only, manual refresh, all service-limit checks and six named checks. The automatic-remediation sentence fails because nothing is enforced, and the API plus weekly-refresh sentence is Business and above, not every plan.

questions.question: A cloud platform group switches AWS Config on across a dozen accounts and writes a short design note for the team. Which claims in that note are accurate?
options: Continuous mode records a configuration item on every change, while Periodic records at best once a day
The recorder writes configuration items to Amazon S3 and notifies through Amazon SNS
A conformance pack deploys a bundle of Config rules and remediation actions as one entity
Managed rules run your own Lambda logic, while custom rules run AWS-published logic
An aggregator keeps each account's results separate and cannot merge them
Turning Config off leaves every Trusted Advisor check working unchanged
questions.explanation: The dossier records that the recorder writes configuration items to Amazon S3 and notifies through Amazon SNS, that Continuous mode writes one per configuration change while Periodic writes at best once every 24 hours and only if the resource changed, and that a conformance pack is a collection of AWS Config rules and remediation actions deployed as a single entity. The rule-type claim is inverted: managed rules are AWS-published and custom rules are your own Lambda logic. The aggregator claim is backwards, since an aggregator is precisely one cross-account, cross-Region view, and some Trusted Advisor checks are powered by AWS Config, so switching Config off degrades that advice.

questions.question: A developer traces how one 1 GB object stays protected under a customer managed KMS key. Put these steps of a write-then-read cycle in order, finishing with what rotation changes.
options: KMS returns a plaintext data key plus that key encrypted under the KMS key
The wrapped data key is stored alongside the ciphertext of the object
Rotation rewraps only the data key, so the 1 GB object is never rewritten
The application encrypts the object with the plaintext key, then discards it
Later, only the wrapped key returns to KMS, which hands back the plaintext key
questions.explanation: The dossier's envelope-encryption sequence: the application calls KMS GenerateDataKey and gets a plaintext data key plus the same key encrypted under the customer managed KMS key, encrypts the 1 GB object with the plaintext key and discards it, stores the wrapped key next to the ciphertext, and later sends only that wrapped key back to KMS Decrypt to recover the plaintext key. Rotating the KMS key changes only the wrapping in that final retrieval, because rotating a key never re-encrypts bulk data, so the decoy about rewriting the object on rotation contradicts the flow.

questions.question: A governance engineer has 40 member accounts to bring under one audit trail. Put these build-out steps in the order they should be executed.
options: Switch on log-file validation and lock the bucket policy to the service role and organization ID
Create a multi-Region organization trail from the management account
Run the lookup query for last quarter's bucket deletions, with principal and source IP
Point one S3 bucket with a folder per account at the trail, plus one CloudWatch Logs group
Confirm member administrators can view the trail but cannot stop or edit it
questions.explanation: The dossier's evidence build-out starts with the management account creating a multi-Region organization trail, then one S3 bucket with a folder per member account ID plus one CloudWatch Logs group receiving everything, then log-file validation staying on with a bucket policy that admits only AWSServiceRoleForCloudTrail and the organization ID, then member admins seeing but never modifying the trail, and only then an Athena or lookup-events query answering which principal deleted which bucket. Running the query before the trail exists leaves nothing to search, and locking the bucket down before the trail writes to it breaks delivery.

questions.question: Match each recurring auditor question to the AWS service whose job that question actually is:
prompts: Is this alarm breaching its threshold right now?
How was this resource configured, and has it drifted?
Where does this account diverge from AWS best practices?
Which user changed this setting, and when did it happen?
Pull every service's findings into one security view?
options: AWS CloudTrail: who did what, and when
Amazon CloudWatch: metrics, thresholds and alarms
AWS Config: configuration state and drift history
AWS Trusted Advisor: best-practice gap checks
AWS Security Hub: aggregated findings and standards
questions.explanation: The dossier's tool-to-question table keys each one by its verb: CloudWatch answers whether the workload is healthy right now through metrics, thresholds and alarms; Config answers how a resource was configured and whether it drifted; Trusted Advisor answers where the account diverges from AWS best practices including MFA on root; CloudTrail answers who performed what action on which resource and when; Security Hub consolidates findings from GuardDuty and others and checks them against security standards. CloudWatch never answers who acted, Config never answers what is breaching a threshold at this moment, and Trusted Advisor cannot consolidate findings from other services.

questions.question: Smartsheet Gov reports going from no presence in AWS GovCloud (US) to FedRAMP ready in under 90 days, a process AWS describes as sometimes taking 12-18 months. The compliance team then asks: 'Where do we obtain the audit report or agreement to hand our assessor?' Which in-scope service answers that question?
options: AWS Artifact: on-demand compliance reports and agreements such as SOC, PCI and ISO documents
AWS Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks across security, cost and service limits, including MFA on the root user
Amazon GuardDuty: threat detection from CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs
AWS Config: configuration state and compliance over time for your own resources
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact is the in-scope service for on-demand compliance reports and agreements: the direct answer to 'where do I get the audit report'. The Smartsheet Gov figure (FedRAMP ready in less than 90 days versus typical 12-18 month timeframes, AWS Public Sector Blog, 29 Aug 2019) is an inheritance-and-evidence story: the controls come from AWS GovCloud (US) and ATO on AWS, but the authorisation and the paperwork stay with the customer. Trusted Advisor checks your account, GuardDuty detects threats and Config tracks your configuration: none of them hands an assessor a third-party compliance document.

questions.question: Socure, an AWS public-sector customer, reports having "inherited over 46 FedRAMP-required security controls from AWS GovCloud (US)" (AWS Public Sector Blog, 14 Nov 2024). Under the shared responsibility model, which statement is correct?
options: Inheritance completes the authorization: once 46 controls are inherited, the workload is FedRAMP authorized with no further customer work

The inherited controls cover AWS's half (physical, environmental and infrastructure controls AWS already evidenced), while the customer still implements and evidences its own controls and obtains the authorization itself: FedRAMP is a government authorization, not an AWS product
AWS GovCloud (US) is a compliance product that automatically issues each customer account a FedRAMP certificate
Inherited controls may be counted twice, so the customer only needs to evidence the remainder of its control set
questions.explanation: Inheritance is the INHERITED category of the control taxonomy: the customer fully inherits AWS's physical, environmental and infrastructure controls, which is why Socure can count 46+ of them. Inheritance reduces the evidence you must produce; it never transfers the obligation. AWS states that no formal certification is available to (or distributable by) a cloud service provider, so the authorization, the remaining controls and the legal responsibility stay with the customer - 'up to 46 inherited' is a work-reduction figure, not an authorization, and it is a customer-claimed number from 14 Nov 2024, not a guarantee.

questions.question: An external auditor asks for proof that the CloudTrail log files delivered to your S3 bucket have not been edited. Which control answers that request?
options: An S3 bucket policy that limits writes to the CloudTrail service role and the organization ID
S3 versioning, which keeps every earlier copy of a file that changes
Amazon CloudWatch Logs retention settings on the trail's log group
Log-file integrity validation, which uses SHA-256 hashing and SHA-256 with RSA signing to chain an hourly digest
questions.explanation: Log-file integrity validation hashes with SHA-256 and signs with SHA-256 with RSA, then writes an hourly digest file chained to the previous digest, which makes it computationally infeasible to modify, delete or forge CloudTrail log files without detection; it is enabled by default for new trails (2.2, log-file integrity validation). Option 0 is the most plausible distractor because a bucket policy controls who may write to the bucket, not whether the bytes already written were altered. Option 2 keeps old copies but never proves the current file is untouched, and option 3 is a retention setting on a log group, which is the consumer pipeline rather than the audit record.

questions.question: A reviewer wants one statement covering object protection in Amazon S3 at rest and API protection in transit, using figures as of Oct 2026. Which is correct?
options: Objects in transit use TLS 1.0 by default for compatibility, and at-rest encryption costs extra unless a customer managed key is selected
Every bucket has been encrypted at rest by default since 5 January 2023 using AES-256 at no extra charge, and AWS APIs require TLS 1.2 while recommending TLS 1.3
At-rest encryption applies only to buckets created after 5 January 2023, and requiring HTTPS for every request needs no policy of any kind
AWS APIs accept plain HTTP until a customer opens a support case, while at-rest encryption is optional for every storage class
questions.explanation: The dossier records both halves: server-side encryption with S3 has been the base level of encryption for every bucket since 5 January 2023 using AES-256 at no extra charge, and AWS APIs require TLS 1.2 while recommending TLS 1.3 (2.2, data protection facts). Option 2 half-succeeds on the date and then fails the enforcement test, because HTTPS-only access is enforced with a bucket policy or an SCP that denies aws:SecureTransport false. Option 0 misstates the transport floor and invents a per-gigabyte charge for the base level, and option 3 contradicts both the default encryption date and the TLS requirement.

questions.question: A compliance analyst sorts AWS's published compliance material into three buckets. Which grouping matches the way AWS presents it as of Oct 2026?
options: Alignments: PCI DSS, FedRAMP, GDPR. Laws: SOC 2, ISO 27001. Certifications: NIST 800-53, CSA STAR
Certifications: HIPAA, DORA. Laws: FIPS 140-3, PCI DSS. Alignments: FedRAMP, IRS 1075
Laws: SOC 1, SOC 2, ISO 27001. Certifications: HIPAA, CJIS. Alignments: FIPS 140-3, FedRAMP
Certifications: SOC, PCI DSS, FedRAMP, FIPS 140-3. Laws: HIPAA, CJIS, DORA. Alignments: NIST 800-53, NIST CSF
questions.explanation: AWS's three buckets are fixed: certifications and attestations are third-party audited material AWS can hold and distribute, covering ISO, SOC, PCI DSS, CSA STAR, FedRAMP, FIPS 140-3 and friends; laws and regulations such as HIPAA, CJIS, FERPA and DORA are the customer's own obligation, with no formal certification available to (or distributable by) a cloud service provider; and alignments are frameworks AWS maps its controls to, namely NIST 800-53 and NIST CSF (2.2, compliance program buckets). Options 1, 2 and 3 all move SOC or ISO documents into the laws column, or push audited certificates into laws or alignments, which reverses the definitions: AWS never certifies a customer to a statute, and an alignment is a control mapping rather than an audit report.

questions.question: A team reviews how AWS CloudTrail behaves before it commits to any paid feature. Which statements are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: Event history is free, automatic and immutable, covers the past 90 days of management events in one Region and cannot be turned off
The first copy of management events delivered to a trail's Amazon S3 bucket is delivered at no charge
Every trail created using the CloudTrail console is a multi-Region trail
Management events are recorded by default from the console, CLI, SDK or another AWS service
Data events are recorded free of charge as soon as a trail exists in the account
A member account can stop or delete an organization trail created by the management account
questions.explanation: The dossier separates event history from a trail: event history is free, automatic, immutable, covers the past 90 days of management events in one Region and cannot be turned off, management events are logged by default with the first copy to S3 free, and all trails created using the CloudTrail console are multi-Region trails (2.2, CloudTrail records actions). Option 4 fails because data events are opt-in and never free, so long retention needs a trail or CloudTrail Lake. Option 5 fails on the organization trail rules: member accounts can see the trail but cannot modify or delete it, because only the management account or a delegated administrator creates it.

questions.question: A landing-zone review checks what AWS Control Tower actually delivers. Which statements are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: A guardrail is a high-level rule expressed in plain language, graded mandatory, strongly recommended or elective
Preventive guardrails are service control policies and resource control policies, so a blocked attempt is denied and logged in CloudTrail
Detective guardrails are AWS Config rules that flag non-compliant resources
Proactive guardrails are CloudFormation hooks evaluated before a resource is created
Mandatory controls can be switched off by any member account that disagrees with them
Control Tower replaces AWS Organizations, so service control policies become unnecessary
questions.explanation: AWS Control Tower governs a multi-account environment by orchestrating AWS Organizations, AWS Service Catalog and AWS IAM Identity Center, where a control equals a guardrail and equals a high-level rule expressed in plain language, graded mandatory, strongly recommended or elective, and the three kinds are preventive (SCPs and RCPs, with the attempt denied and logged in CloudTrail), detective (AWS Config rules flagging non-compliant resources) and proactive (CloudFormation hooks evaluated before the resource is created) (2.2, Control Tower guardrails). Option 4 inverts the grading: mandatory controls are always applied and cannot be changed, and no member account opts out. Option 5 has the relationship backwards, because Control Tower builds on top of Organizations and an organization without service control policies has no preventive guardrails at all.

questions.question: A governance lead sequences the build-out for a fresh multi-account estate. Put these steps in the order the lesson gives.
options: Add the AWS-managed FullAWSAccess service control policy, then your own deny-only policies
Add the evidence layer: an organization trail in CloudTrail plus AWS Config rules and conformance packs
Consolidate every member account into the management account so that one policy covers them all
Create the organization: one root, organizational units and member accounts
Lay down the landing zone with AWS Control Tower: Account Factory, mandatory guardrails, dashboard
Enable all features so that service control policies and tag policies become available
questions.explanation: The dossier's governance build-out runs in fixed order: create the organization with one root, OUs and member accounts; enable all features so SCPs and tag policies become available; attach the AWS-managed FullAWSAccess SCP and then your own deny-only policies; lay down the landing zone with AWS Control Tower and Account Factory; add the evidence layer of an organization trail plus AWS Config rules and conformance packs; then standardise tags and activate cost allocation tags (2.2, governance build-out). Option 2 is the trap in the list: SCPs do not affect users or roles in the management account, so parking every member account there would exempt the estate from the very policies you are attaching, and OU membership alone restricts nothing.

questions.question: A team switches on AWS Config and asks how one compliance question gets answered end to end. Put these stages in the order they happen.
options: A rule stamps each resource compliant or non-compliant against your ideal configuration settings
Remediation acts through an AWS Systems Manager document
The configuration recorder captures a change in the account
An aggregator presents one cross-account, cross-Region view of compliance
Configuration items are written to Amazon S3 and Amazon SNS is notified
questions.explanation: The dossier's mechanics are sequential: the recorder writes configuration items to Amazon S3 and notifies through Amazon SNS while assuming an IAM role, then a Config rule encodes your ideal configuration settings and the engine stamps each resource compliant or non-compliant, remediation can run through an AWS Systems Manager document, and an aggregator gives one cross-account, cross-Region view of configuration and compliance (2.2, AWS Config mechanics and Config rules). Reading the aggregator first, or the rule before the recorder, reverses the flow: no rule can judge a resource whose changes were never recorded, and remediation has nothing to act on until a resource has been stamped non-compliant.

questions.question: Match each AWS Config rule type to who creates it and what runs inside it:
prompts: Managed rule
Custom rule
Service-linked rule
Organizational rule
options: Published by AWS, ready to use without writing code
Deployed across an organization from the management account
Runs your own evaluation logic inside an AWS Lambda function
Created and maintained by an AWS service on your behalf
questions.explanation: AWS Config has exactly four rule types: Managed rules are AWS-published, Custom rules run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, Service-linked rules are created and maintained by an AWS service, and Organizational rules are deployed across an organization from the management account (2.2, AWS Config rules). The inversion trap is the one to watch: a managed rule never executes your Lambda code, and a custom rule is not AWS-published logic, because the whole point of the custom type is that the evaluation function is yours. On top of these types sit conformance packs and aggregators, which package rules and roll up results rather than defining who writes the rule.

questions.question: A company has 12 AWS accounts and 400 employees, while a separate consumer app needs customer sign-up and limited access to S3. Which pairing is correct?
options: Employees: IAM Identity Center with permission sets and one login; customers: Amazon Cognito user pool for authentication plus an identity pool for temporary AWS credentials
Employees: a shared IAM user per department; customers: AWS Directory Service Simple AD
Employees: Amazon Cognito user pools; customers: IAM Identity Center permission sets
Employees: IAM users in every account with the same password; customers: root user credentials for the app
questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center is the workforce answer: one login across many accounts, federated identity source, permission sets that become roles with temporary credentials. Cognito is customer identity: the user pool is the directory plus authentication (issuing JWTs), and the identity pool exchanges a token for temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials via STS. Directory Service is enterprise Active Directory, and sharing IAM users: or using root: is never correct.

questions.question: A lead proposes attaching a service control policy (SCP) to give an audit team read-only access to a member account. Why is this wrong?
options: SCPs can only be attached to IAM users, not to organizational units
SCPs never grant permissions: they only filter what an identity in the account could otherwise do, and the audit team still needs an identity or role that allows the actions
SCPs apply only to the root user of the management account
SCPs are resource-based policies and therefore cannot name a principal in another account
questions.explanation: SCPs are a ceiling: they intersect with whatever the identity is allowed, and they grant nothing on their own. Access still requires an identity-based policy or a role in the member account, plus (for cross-account) an allow on both sides. SCPs attach to OUs, accounts or the root of an organization: not to IAM users.

questions.question: A team lead asks which of the following actions can ONLY be performed by the account root user. Which answer is correct?
options: Enabling MFA Delete on an S3 bucket, and creating an administrative IAM user
Attaching a permissions policy to an IAM group, and closing a standalone account
Changing the root password and access keys, closing a standalone account, and restoring IAM user permissions after a last-administrator lockout
Stopping an Amazon EC2 instance and enabling Amazon GuardDuty
questions.explanation: Root-only tasks include managing the root credentials themselves, closing or reopening a standalone account, restoring IAM user permissions (the lockout recovery), activating IAM access to billing, viewing certain tax invoices, EC2 Reserved Instances Marketplace registration and S3 MFA Delete. Creating IAM users and attaching policies are normal administrative tasks, and stopping EC2 or enabling GuardDuty never requires root.

questions.question: An IAM identity policy allows s3:GetObject on reports/*, but the bucket policy denies s3:* whenever aws:SecureTransport is false, and the request is made over plain HTTP. What is the result?
options: Allowed: the identity policy is evaluated first and identity policies take precedence over resource policies
Denied - AWS first checks all applicable policies for an explicit Deny, and one Deny beats every Allow
Allowed: identity-based and resource-based policies are combined by intersection, and the identity Allow is enough
Denied: all S3 bucket policies automatically deny non-HTTPS requests regardless of any policy content
questions.explanation: AWS evaluates by collecting every applicable policy and checking for an explicit Deny first; a single Deny in any applicable document wins over all Allows. Identity and resource policies form a UNION (either can allow), not an intersection, and nothing is denied merely because it is an S3 request: the bucket policy text is what denies it.

questions.question: An application running on Amazon EC2 must read objects from one S3 bucket, and no long-term credentials may be shipped with the code. Which design fits the exam's best practice?
options: Create an IAM user with one access key, store the secret in the application configuration, and rotate it once a year

Create a role that trusts ec2.amazonaws.com with a policy allowing s3:GetObject on that bucket only, and attach it to the instance through an instance profile so temporary credentials are auto-refreshed from the metadata service
Use the account root access keys so the application never runs out of permissions
Attach an AWS managed administrator policy to the instance role to avoid future permission changes
questions.explanation: Roles plus an instance profile give the workload temporary security credentials that refresh automatically, with a blast radius defined by a narrow policy. Access keys are long-term (maximum two per IAM user) and must not be embedded, root access keys should never exist, and attaching an administrator policy violates the principle of least privilege.

questions.question: A compliance reviewer audits how the team uses IAM and drafts six statements. Which of them are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: An IAM group can share one identity policy with several users, but the group holds no credentials and cannot appear as a Principal
An IAM role pairs a permissions policy with a trust policy and hands out temporary security credentials through AWS STS
A permissions boundary is a managed policy that sets the maximum an identity policy may grant, and it grants nothing by itself
A resource-based policy sits on the resource itself, is always inline, and can name a principal in another AWS account
IAM groups nest up to five levels deep, and every new account ships with a default group of administrators
Attaching a permissions boundary to the account narrows every existing IAM user policy automatically
questions.explanation: The dossier's IAM object list keys statements 0 to 3: a group is a collection of users sharing one identity policy, with no credentials, no nesting, no default group and no place as a Principal; a role is a permissions policy plus a trust policy that yields STS temporary security credentials; a boundary is a ceiling that grants nothing on its own; and resource-based policies live on the resource, are inline only and may name a cross-account principal (2.3, IAM objects and boundaries). Statement 4 borrows the five-level nesting limit, which belongs to organizational units in AWS Organizations, not to groups, and no default group exists (numeric bait). Statement 5 flips what a boundary is: because it grants nothing by itself, it cannot narrow anyone's existing policy; its exam job is safe delegation.

questions.question: A security lead has a backlog of over-broad permissions policies to close this quarter. Which moves actually narrow them?
options: Start from an AWS managed job-function policy, then delete the actions the identity never performs
Generate a candidate policy from the account's CloudTrail activity with IAM Access Analyzer and trim it to the buckets and actions actually used
Drop the permissions that last-accessed information shows nobody has used in months
Attach the same AWS managed administrator policy to every new role, because AWS maintains it and it never needs review
Rewrite the permissions as inline policies, since inline policies are maintained by AWS on your behalf
Turn on CloudTrail and wait, because recording API activity revokes the permissions nobody uses
questions.explanation: The least-privilege toolkit in the dossier is exactly 0 to 2: begin from a broad AWS managed job-function policy and carve it down, let IAM Access Analyzer generate a policy from CloudTrail activity and preview exposure, then use last-accessed information to delete permissions nobody uses (2.3, least-privilege narrowing). Option 3 over-claims: AWS managed policies are broad starting points, so attaching an administrator policy everywhere is the opposite of narrowing. Option 4 is a responsibility flip: inline policies are embedded in the principal and deleted with it, and they are dangerous as a default, not AWS-maintained. Option 5 is true-but-irrelevant: CloudTrail records the activity that feeds the next narrowing pass, but nothing in a trail revokes a permission by itself.

questions.question: A platform team is writing up how AWS decides whether one API request is allowed. Put the steps in the order AWS evaluates them.
options: Union the identity-based and resource-based allows, because either document can allow the action
Authenticate the caller, then collect every applicable policy: identity-based, resource-based, SCP, RCP, permissions boundary and session policy
Intersect the identity policy with the service control policy first, then look for a Deny
Check every collected policy for an explicit Deny; a single Deny ends the evaluation
Intersect the union with the ceilings, so the permissions boundary, SCP and RCP must all allow
Return implicit deny when no policy allows the action
questions.explanation: The dossier's evaluation order is: authenticate the caller, gather every applicable policy, let any explicit Deny win immediately, union the identity-based and resource-based allows, then intersect that union with the ceilings (permissions boundary, SCP and RCP must all allow), and fall back to implicit deny when nothing allows (2.3, policy evaluation). Option 2 is the trap step: it looks for the Deny only after an intersection, but AWS first checks all policies for a Deny, and an SCP is a ceiling that intersects later rather than a partner for the identity policy, because service control policies filter and never grant. Option 0 is a true step, but it belongs third, not first: union runs only after the Deny check.

questions.question: An outside analytics firm needs read-only access to production account 2222 from its own account 1111. Sequence the build.
options: In account 1111, attach an identity policy to the firm's group allowing sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN
In account 2222, create AuditorRole whose trust policy allows sts:AssumeRole for account 1111 with an external ID
In account 1111, create an IAM user per auditor and hand out long-term access keys
In account 2222, attach the read-only permissions policy to AuditorRole
questions.explanation: The dossier's cross-account audit role build runs in this order: create the role in 2222 with a resource-based trust policy naming account 1111 and an external ID because a third party is involved, attach the role's read-only permissions policy in 2222, then attach an identity policy in 1111 that allows sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN (2.3, cross-account role). Either policy alone fails: trust without the identity grant returns not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRole, and an identity grant without trust returns you are not authorized. The distractor step is the anti-pattern: long-term access keys shipped to an external firm are exactly what roles replace, since the resulting session is temporary and expires on its own.

questions.question: Match each credential need the security team describes to the mechanism the exam expects:
prompts: A database password that application code reads when it starts
A build pipeline parameter injected at deploy time, encrypted at rest
Long-term CLI access for a legacy tool that cannot assume roles
A role session that must expire by itself inside 12 hours
A phishing-resistant factor for administrator sign-in
Identities that already live in the corporate directory
options: STS temporary security credentials
AWS Directory Service
Passkey or FIDO security key
AWS Secrets Manager
IAM access keys, maximum two per user
Systems Manager Parameter Store
questions.explanation: Task 2.3 names credential storage and the authentication options in the dossier: secrets live in AWS Secrets Manager or AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (SecureString), access keys are long-term with a maximum of two per IAM user, STS temporary credentials last minutes to 12 hours, passkeys and FIDO security keys are the phishing-resistant recommended factors, and Directory Service covers enterprise directory identities (2.3, credential options). The traps: access keys are the legacy fallback, not the answer for a session that must expire, because they are long-term and the secret is shown only once; and SMS MFA is no longer offered in IAM, so any choice resting on text-message codes is stale.

questions.question: A developer wants a third long-lived CLI credential because two tools already hold one key each. Which statement about AWS access keys is correct as of Oct 2026?
options: An IAM user can hold at most two access keys at a time, and the secret access key is shown only once at creation
An IAM user can hold unlimited access keys, and AWS stores every secret so it can be displayed again later
Access keys are temporary credentials that expire by themselves within 12 hours
Access keys should be created for the account root user so that every tool shares one identity
questions.explanation: The dossier's credential rules key option 0: an IAM user is a permanent identity in one account with long-term credentials, capped at two access keys so key one can be rotated while key two is still live, and the secret key is shown only once (2.3, authentication and credential options). Option 1 is wrong because a secret that was not kept cannot be re-displayed, which is why rotation keeps a second key handy. Option 2 describes AWS STS temporary credentials, which run from minutes up to 12 hours, not access keys. Option 3 is wrong because root access keys are never recommended: root exists for root-only tasks.

questions.question: An engineer assumes an IAM role in a second account and asks how long the resulting credentials remain valid. Which statement is correct as of Oct 2026?
options: The session lasts 24 hours by default and cannot be shortened by the trust policy
The session lasts 1 hour by default and can be extended to at most 12 hours, while role chaining is capped at 1 hour
Credentials from AWS Security Token Service never expire as long as the calling identity still exists
The target account's root user picks an expiry date after the role has been assumed
questions.explanation: The dossier's session arithmetic is explicit: AssumeRole sessions last up to 43,200 seconds, that is 12 hours, with a 1-hour default, and role chaining is capped at 1 hour (2.3, roles versus users). Option 0 inverts both figures. Option 2 is the anti-pattern the exam tests by inversion: the whole reason roles replace access keys is that STS credentials expire on their own. Option 3 invents a root control that does not exist: the trust policy names who may assume the role, and the resulting permissions replace the caller's for the life of the session.

questions.question: A company wants employees to sign in through its existing SAML 2.0 identity provider and reach many AWS accounts with one login. Which statement about IAM Identity Center is correct as of Oct 2026?
options: It replaces IAM, so identity policies and IAM roles are deleted as soon as it is enabled
It is the customer sign-up directory for an application, issuing JSON Web Tokens to end users

It was renamed from AWS Single Sign-On on 26 July 2022, delivers permissions through permission sets with no long-term keys, accepts the built-in directory or an external SAML 2.0 or OIDC identity source, and uses IAM roles underneath
It requires one IAM user in every account, each sharing the same password
questions.explanation: The dossier's Identity Center facts key option 2: workforce single sign-on renamed from AWS Single Sign-On on 26 July 2022, one login across many accounts, permission sets instead of long-term keys, identity source either the built-in directory or an external SAML 2.0 or OIDC provider, IAM roles underneath and IAM not replaced (2.3, IAM Identity Center). Option 0 fails on the last clause. Option 1 describes Amazon Cognito, whose user pool authenticates an application's customers. Option 3 is the pattern the service exists to eliminate: 12 accounts and 400 employees means federation, not a user per account.

questions.question: A team must let an AWS service create and manage resources in its account on the team's behalf. Which mechanism does the exam expect?
options: An IAM user dedicated to that service, holding two long-lived access keys stored beside the application
The account root access keys, because a service acting on your behalf needs the widest permissions
A resource-based policy attached to the service itself, since AWS services cannot assume roles
A service role or service-linked role whose trust policy lets the service assume it, so it acts with temporary credentials
questions.explanation: The dossier maps the use case directly: a service acting on your behalf gets a service role or a service-linked role (2.3, roles versus users by use case). A role is a permissions policy plus a trust policy that yields AWS STS temporary security credentials, so the service refreshes them instead of holding a key. Option 0 is the anti-pattern roles replace: long-lived keys in an application. Option 1 is wrong because root access keys should never exist. Option 2 gets the mechanics backwards: services do assume roles, and it is the trust policy on the role that names them.

questions.question: One AWS Lambda function writes objects to exactly one bucket named reports-archive. Which permissions statement follows least privilege?
options: Allow s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::reports-archive/* and nothing else
Allow the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy, because AWS maintains it for you
Allow s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject on every bucket, because cleanup may be needed later
Allow s3:* on arn:aws:s3:::* so that future buckets need no policy change
questions.explanation: Least privilege means the smallest bucket and the smallest action set that the workload actually uses, and the dossier's worked example fixes exactly this shape: one policy allowing s3:* on * is narrowed with IAM Access Analyzer to specific buckets and actions (2.3, least-privilege narrowing). Option 0 grants on every bucket in the account, the widest statement on the list. Option 2 pads the grant with delete rights the function never exercises, and later use is not a reason to pre-grant. Option 3 mistakes an AWS managed policy for a finished policy: managed job-function policies are broad starting points that you then carve down, and AdministratorAccess is the opposite of least privilege.

questions.question: A compliance officer drafts a standard for protecting the AWS account root user. Which statements in that standard are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: The root password runs 8 to 128 characters with at least 3 of 4 character classes and must not match the account name or email
MFA is registered within 35 days of first sign-in, up to 8 devices in any mix, using passkeys or FIDO security keys, virtual authenticator TOTP or hardware TOTP
Root access keys are never created, and multi-person approval keeps the password with one group and the MFA device with a different group
SMS MFA is enabled on the root user, because AWS still sends one-time codes by text message
A second root user is created as a backup identity so that one can be frozen during an incident
Root access keys are kept in a sealed envelope for emergencies, because root cannot use MFA
questions.explanation: Options 0 to 2 restate the dossier's root credential safeguards: password 8 to 128 characters with 3 of 4 classes that must not match the account name or email, MFA registered within 35 days of first sign-in with up to 8 devices in any mix and passkeys or FIDO keys plus virtual or hardware TOTP as the supported factors, zero root access keys, and AWS's recommendation of multi-person approval splitting the password and the MFA device (2.3, root credential safeguards). Option 3 is stale: SMS MFA is no longer offered in IAM, so any answer resting on text-message codes fails. Option 4 is impossible because exactly one root identity exists per account and it cannot be deleted. Option 5 contradicts the same rule as option 3's companion trap: root access keys are never recommended, and MFA does work for root.

questions.question: A platform lead reviews a proposal to give every engineer and every application its own long-lived IAM user. Which statements in the review are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: An IAM user is a permanent identity in one account with long-term credentials, so the recommended pattern stays federation for humans and roles for workloads
An IAM user remains acceptable for a legacy or break-glass account, and for third-party AWS tools with no IAM Identity Center support
An IAM user holds at most two access keys at a time, and its secret access key is shown only once
Roles cannot cross account boundaries, so every account needs its own IAM user
Application keys may live in a public AWS Lambda function's environment variables as long as those variables are never printed to the log
Deleting an access key makes it expire on its own after 12 hours, exactly like a role session
questions.explanation: The dossier supports 0 to 2: an IAM user is permanent with long-term credentials in one account, so AWS's wording is to require human users to use federation and give workloads roles; an IAM user is the documented exception for a legacy or break-glass account or a third-party AWS tool with no Identity Center support; and a user holds a maximum of two access keys with the secret shown once (2.3, IAM objects and credential options). Option 3 is false on the highest-yield sentence in Domain 2: roles are the primary way to grant cross-account access. Option 4 is the hard-coded secrets anti-pattern; secrets belong in AWS Secrets Manager or AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (SecureString). Option 5 confuses long-term keys, which never expire on their own, with STS temporary credentials.

questions.question: A security lead stands up a brand-new AWS account and writes the day-one hardening runbook. Put these steps in the order the dossier gives them.
options: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail to a private bucket with log-file validation, then switch on AWS Config and Amazon GuardDuty
Point the root email address at a group alias such as aws-root at company dot com rather than a personal mailbox
Add an Amazon EventBridge rule on root sign-in that pushes a notification to Amazon SNS
Hand out long-lived root access keys to the two administrators who will need them
Place the administrative identity in IAM Identity Center for a multi-account setup, or in an admin IAM user for a single account
Attach an AWS Organizations service control policy that denies member-account root actions
questions.explanation: The dossier's day-1 root hardening order runs: root email alias, then root password, then MFA, then no access keys, then the administrative identity, then the CloudTrail trail with log-file validation plus Config and GuardDuty, then the EventBridge rule on root sign-in to SNS, and finally, inside an organization, stripped member-account root credentials or an SCP denying member-account root actions (2.3, day-1 root hardening). Steps 1, 4, 0, 2 and 5 preserve that published order. The distractor step is wrong twice over: root access keys are never created, and AWS's wording is that one group holds the account password while a different group holds the MFA device.

questions.question: An operations team wants to rebuild its access model the way the least-privilege cycle sequences it. Put these steps in order, foundation first.
options: Start from an AWS managed job-function policy, then narrow it with IAM Access Analyzer and last-accessed information
Create an IAM user for every engineer and hand out access keys, then add protections afterwards
Require human users to use federation with temporary credentials
Give workloads IAM roles instead of long-lived access keys
Turn on AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector and Amazon Macie so that detection data feeds the next pass
Protect the root user with MFA and no access keys
questions.explanation: The dossier's least-privilege cycle is foundation first: protect the root user with MFA and no access keys, require human users to use federation with temporary credentials, give workloads roles instead of access keys, start from an AWS managed job-function policy, narrow it with IAM Access Analyzer and last-accessed data, then turn on CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie so detection feeds the next narrowing pass (2.3, least-privilege cycle). The distractor reverses the foundation: identity hygiene comes first, and least privilege is a cycle rather than a clean-up project that starts with one IAM user per engineer.

questions.question: Match each access need the architect describes to the mechanism the dossier pairs with it:
prompts: An EC2 workload that reads one bucket with no shipped keys
Read-only access to account 2222 from account 1111
Employees signing in through the corporate SAML provider
An external auditor, with a third party involved
A service that must act on the account's behalf
A legacy tool that cannot assume roles and needs CLI access
options: IAM Identity Center permission sets with no long-term keys
A trusting-account role allowed by the caller's identity policy
A role with an external ID in its trust policy
An instance profile that refreshes temporary credentials
A service-linked role that the service assumes
An IAM user with two long-lived access keys
questions.explanation: The dossier's roles-versus-users table decides every pair: a workload on EC2 gets an instance profile whose credentials refresh from the instance metadata service; cross-account access needs a role in the trusting account plus an sts:AssumeRole allow in the caller's identity policy, because both sides must allow; human federation uses IAM Identity Center permission sets or a SAML 2.0 or OIDC provider; an external third party needs an external ID in the trust policy as the confused-deputy defence; a service acting on your behalf gets a service-linked role; and only a legacy or break-glass tool that cannot assume roles justifies an IAM user with long-lived keys, capped at two (2.3, roles versus users). The swaps that cost marks: a trust policy alone grants no actions, an identity grant alone cannot be assumed, and access keys are what roles replace.

questions.question: A security engineer asks which service records every API call made in the account, including the caller, the time and the source IP. Which service BEST answers that question?
options: AWS CloudTrail, because actions taken by a user, role or AWS service are recorded as events
AWS Trusted Advisor, because it identifies security issues in the account
Amazon CloudWatch, because it stores every log the account produces
AWS Config, because it records the state of every resource
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records actions: events with an identity, action, time and source: across console, CLI, SDK and AWS-service calls, which AWS names as enabling operational and risk auditing, governance and compliance. CloudWatch handles metrics and alarms, Trusted Advisor recommends fixes, and Config records configuration state rather than API calls.

questions.question: A security team wants free, automatic DDoS protection for its AWS workloads with no subscription and no configuration. Which statement matches AWS's documentation?
options: Enable Shield Advanced first, then downgrade to Shield Standard if no attack occurs
Purchase AWS Firewall Manager, which includes free DDoS protection for all accounts

Shield Standard is provided automatically and at no extra charge; Shield Advanced is the paid option with a 1-year commitment, DDoS cost protection and the Shield Response Team, which requires Business or Enterprise Support
Subscribe to Shield Standard and configure its mitigation rules
questions.explanation: Shield Standard comes automatically at no extra charge and cannot be subscribed to or configured. Shield Advanced costs 3,000 USD/month per payer with a 1-year commitment (as of Oct 2026), adds automatic Layer 7 mitigation, DDoS cost protection and up to 50 billion WAF requests per month, and its Shield Response Team requires Business or Enterprise Support. Firewall Manager manages policy across an organization; it is not the DDoS protection itself.

questions.question: A team provisions 1 AWS WAF web ACL with 5 rules and inspects 10 million requests in a month. Using the pricing components verified for this lesson (as of Oct 2026), what is the monthly total?
options: 16.00 USD - 5 USD for the web ACL, 5 USD for the rules and 6 USD for the requests
11.00 USD: rules are free and only the ACL and requests are billed
30.00 USD: AWS always bills the published 19-rule example total
60.00 USD: WAF bills 5 USD per rule plus a flat 55 USD request fee
questions.explanation: The verified components are 5.00 USD per web ACL per month, 1.00 USD per rule per month and 0.60 USD per 1 million requests: 5 USD + (5 x 1 USD) + (10 x 0.60 USD) = 16.00 USD. AWS's own worked example with 19 rules and 10 million requests totals 30.00 USD, and security groups and network ACLs remain free: so neither 30.00 USD nor a rule-free total is correct here.

questions.question: An auditor asks: 'Was port 3306 open to 0.0.0.0/0 on 1 March, and when did it close?' Which service can answer?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor, because it checks for unrestricted security-group ports
AWS CloudTrail, because it logs every AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress call
Amazon CloudWatch, because it alarms on security-group changes
AWS Config, because continuous recording stores configuration items that show how the security group was configured over time
questions.explanation: This is a configuration-state-over-a-period question, which only AWS Config answers through configuration items captured by the recorder. CloudTrail records that a change was made (the action), Trusted Advisor advises on the current gap, and CloudWatch monitors metrics: none of them reconstruct a duration.

questions.question: Which set of statements about AWS KMS key types is correct (as of Oct 2026)?
options: AWS owned keys live in your account and can be deleted on a schedule; customer managed keys are free of monthly charges
AWS managed keys are stored outside your account and customer managed keys never rotate
All three key types are identical in control, and only the alias differs

Customer managed keys carry a monthly fee plus usage charges and give you key-policy control; AWS managed keys use aliases like aws/ebs, rotate about every 365 days, have no monthly key fee and cannot be deleted by you; AWS owned keys are neither visible nor auditable by you
questions.explanation: Customer managed keys are yours: key policy control, enable/disable, scheduled deletion and custom rotation, billed monthly (hourly prorated) plus usage. AWS managed keys live in your account under aliases such as aws/ebs, rotate about every 365 days, have no monthly key fee and cannot be edited or deleted by you. AWS owned keys belong to the service's own account: free, invisible and undeletable by you.

questions.question: A team debugging why its default VPC filtering allows more traffic than expected records six claims. Which are true as of Oct 2026?
options: The default security group allows all outbound traffic and inbound traffic only from itself
The default network ACL allows all traffic in and out, with its star DENY rules sitting at the bottom of the list
Neither layer filters DNS, DHCP, the instance metadata service or ECS task metadata
A security group can reference another security group, while a network ACL cannot
A deny rule can be added to the security group to block a known-bad range
The default network ACL denies every packet that no rule explicitly allows, because its star DENY rules evaluate first
questions.explanation: The dossier's filter defaults and bypasses key 0 to 3: the default security group allows all outbound and inbound only from itself, the default network ACL allows all traffic in and out with the star DENY rules at the bottom of the list, neither layer filters DNS, DHCP, the instance metadata service or ECS task metadata, and only security groups can reference other security groups (2.4, filter defaults). Claim 4 is the layer error the lesson flags as always wrong: security groups are allow-only, so a known-bad range belongs in a network ACL deny rule. Claim 5 reverses the default network ACL twice: it is permissive by default, and although numbered rules with first match are a network ACL property, the star DENY entries sit last, not first.

questions.question: A holding company wants one rule set pushed to every subsidiary account before those accounts launch workloads. Which statements about AWS Firewall Manager are correct?
options: It requires AWS Organizations to be enabled, and it manages WAF, Shield Advanced, security group and network ACL policies across the organization
Resources created after a policy is pushed are covered automatically, with no second configuration pass
It costs 100 US dollars per policy per Region per month as of Oct 2026
It pushes policy to accounts rather than inspecting packets or filtering traffic itself
It is free of charge, because Shield Standard already includes organization-wide policy management
It can be attached to a single IAM user, so only that user's resources receive the rules
questions.explanation: The dossier describes Firewall Manager as an organization-wide policy pusher: AWS Organizations must be enabled, it manages WAF, Shield Advanced, security group and network ACL policies across the organization, it auto-covers new resources, and it costs 100 US dollars per policy per Region per month as of Oct 2026 (2.4, Firewall Manager). Option 4 pairs a true fact with a false one: Shield Standard is free and automatic, but it is Layer 3/4 DDoS protection, not policy management, so it cannot make a management service free. Option 5 reverses the scope: Firewall Manager works at the organization and OU level through policies, never per IAM user, and its phrasing test is apply this rule set to every account in the organization.

questions.question: A solutions architect is sequencing a layered network defence from the outside in. Place the steps in the order the lesson gives.
options: Security group on the database tier allowing 5432 from the application security group only
Network ACL at the public subnet edge denying a known-bad CIDR in numbered rule 100
Allow port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 on the database security group so administrators can connect
Security group on the application load balancer allowing 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 only
AWS WAF web ACL on the load balancer with managed rules and a rate-based rule
Security group on the application tier allowing 8080 from the load balancer security group
questions.explanation: The dossier's layered defence runs outermost to innermost: security group on the load balancer for 443, security group on the app tier referencing the load balancer security group, security group on the database for 5432 from the app tier, then the network ACL at the subnet edge with a numbered deny for a known-bad CIDR, then the AWS WAF web ACL on the load balancer (2.4, layered network defence). Security group referencing is what makes step 5 follow step 3, and numbered rules with first-match are a network ACL property, which is why the deny belongs there and not in a security group. The distractor step is disqualified by the defence-in-depth checklist, which scores 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 as a finding: fix it with a bastion security group or SSM Session Manager instead.

questions.question: Match each finding the security operations team receives to the AWS service that produces it:
prompts: Correlates CloudTrail, VPC flow logs and DNS logs for threat intel
Scans workloads and container images for known CVEs and exposure
Finds sensitive data such as PII and credentials inside S3 buckets
Builds a behaviour graph so an analyst can trace a root cause
Consolidates findings, then checks them against security standards
options: Amazon Macie
AWS Security Hub
Amazon Detective
Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Inspector
questions.explanation: The dossier's one-liners decide every pair: GuardDuty detects by correlating CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs with threat intelligence and machine learning; Inspector scans EC2, container images and functions for CVEs and network exposure; Macie finds sensitive data in S3 with machine learning and pattern matching; Detective builds a behaviour graph for investigation; Security Hub aggregates and prioritises findings and checks them against standards (2.4, security service jobs).
