questions.question: A healthcare company runs hundreds of VPCs across 120 accounts and needs one hub that interconnects them with each other and with an on-premises data center over a dedicated link with consistent bandwidth. Which pair of CLF-C02 in-scope services delivers that design?
options: A full mesh of VPC peering connections plus a NAT gateway to carry the on-premises traffic
AWS Transit Gateway for the many VPCs plus AWS Direct Connect for the dedicated on-premises link
AWS Site-to-Site VPN alone plus AWS PrivateLink for whole-VPC connectivity between accounts
Amazon CloudFront plus Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing to place the traffic
questions.explanation: Peering is a strict one-to-one, non-transitive relationship, so a mesh of peerings is exactly what AWS built Transit Gateway (0.05 USD per attachment-hour plus 0.02 USD per GB processed) to replace when many VPCs and on-premises networks meet in one hub. Direct Connect is the dedicated private circuit with consistent bandwidth: weeks to provision and NOT encrypted by default. Site-to-Site VPN is encrypted and fast to build but is a best-effort internet tunnel rather than a dedicated link, PrivateLink exposes a single service rather than whole VPCs, and CloudFront plus Route 53 are edge and DNS services, not VPC interconnect. Note that the real athenahealth case also used AWS Network Firewall, which sits on the out-of-scope list as of Oct 2026 and can only appear as a distractor.

questions.question: A web application needs host-based and path-based routing, HTTPS termination, AWS WAF protection, and must be spread across at least two Availability Zones. Which load balancer fits?
options: Network Load Balancer - Layer 4 with flow hashing and a static IP per Availability Zone
Application Load Balancer - Layer 7 listener rules routing to target groups, with WAF support and a minimum of two enabled Availability Zones
Classic Load Balancer: the previous generation that AWS recommends migrating away from
Route 53 multivalue answer routing, which returns up to eight healthy records at random
questions.explanation: Only the ALB operates at Layer 7 with listener rules on host and path, supports AWS WAF, and formally requires at least two enabled Availability Zones. The NLB is Layer 4 with no host or path rules and no WAF, the Classic Load Balancer is explicitly called the previous generation, and Route 53 cannot perform target-level health-checked routing for an application.

questions.question: A cloud engineer reviews a freshly built VPC and records five claims about its topology and its visibility tooling. Which statements are accurate as the networking lesson documents them?
options: A subnet belongs to exactly one Availability Zone and is public only if its route table carries a route to an internet gateway
A route table is an ordered list of destination CIDR to target routes, exactly one is associated per subnet, and longest prefix match wins
VPC flow logs capture metadata of allowed and rejected traffic rather than the packet payload
Attaching an internet gateway to the VPC immediately makes every subnet in that VPC public
An Elastic IP address costs nothing while it sits unattached, because no data flows through it
VPC flow logs retain full packet payloads, so an incident can be replayed frame by frame
questions.explanation: The lesson documents all three keyed statements: a subnet sits in exactly one Availability Zone and is public if and only if its route table carries a route to an internet gateway; a route table is an ordered list of destination CIDR to target routes with exactly one associated per subnet and longest prefix match deciding the winner; and VPC flow logs capture metadata of allowed and rejected traffic, not the payload. The internet-gateway claim fails because attaching the gateway changes no subnet until the 0.0.0.0/0 to igw route is written into that subnet's route table. The Elastic IP claim fails on the idle-resource trap: static public IPv4 is charged in use AND idle at 0.005 US dollars per hour, about 3.65 US dollars per month, whether or not traffic flows. The payload claim fails on the same fact that keys the third option: flow logs hold metadata only, so there is never a frame to replay.

questions.question: Match each DNS requirement to the Amazon Route 53 element that satisfies it, using the record and hosted-zone rules the networking lesson documents:
prompts: Point a name at one other hostname and never at the zone apex
Answer at the zone apex for a load balancer without query charges
Hold records that anyone on the internet can resolve worldwide
Hold records resolvable only from inside the VPCs you attach
Watch an endpoint or a CloudWatch alarm to drive DNS failover
options: A private hosted zone, resolvable only within attached VPCs
A public hosted zone, 0.50 USD per month for the first 25 zones
A Route 53 health check targeting an endpoint or a CloudWatch alarm
A CNAME record, which DNS bars from the zone apex
A Route 53 alias record, with no charge for queries to AWS targets
questions.explanation: Each prompt quotes a documented Route 53 rule: a CNAME cannot sit at the zone apex while an alias record can, and alias records that point at AWS targets such as load balancers incur no charge for the queries; a public hosted zone is resolvable on the internet at 0.50 US dollars per month for the first 25 zones, with 10,000 records included; a private hosted zone is resolvable only within one or more VPCs, and queries inside the VPC are free; and a health check can target an endpoint, another health check or a CloudWatch alarm, which is what drives DNS failover. The near misses fail on scope: a public hosted zone is internet-resolvable rather than VPC-restricted, a health check monitors a resource instead of storing records, and a CNAME is barred from the apex exactly because the alias record exists to cover that job.

questions.question: A Linux application needs a boot volume, sustained database IOPS, and the ability to snapshot for restore. Which block-storage answer is correct?
options: Instance store, because it offers the highest local I/O and survives an instance stop
An st1 throughput-optimized HDD volume, because HDD is always the cheapest boot option
A gp3 volume for boot plus io2 where a provisioned IOPS ceiling is required, backed by incremental snapshots
An S3 Glacier Deep Archive mount, because archive classes can be attached to EC2
questions.explanation: gp3 is the default boot-capable SSD with 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any volume size; io1/io2 (io2 Block Express up to 256,000 IOPS, 99.999% durability) answer a mission-critical IOPS ceiling. Snapshots are incremental and AWS does NOT automatically back up EBS volumes. Instance store loses all data when the instance is stopped and cannot be snapshotted, st1 and sc1 cannot be boot volumes, and S3 cannot be mounted as a block device.

questions.question: An operations team needs to overwrite-and-audit objects, automatically delete expired ones, and make sure deleting an object does not destroy its history. Which combination delivers that?
options: Enable versioning for history, add a lifecycle rule with expiration and noncurrent-version expiration actions, and rely on delete markers instead of hard deletes
Enable replication only, because replication deletes old versions automatically
Turn off encryption, because encrypted objects cannot be expired
Use S3 One Zone-IA, which stores a second copy in another AZ
questions.explanation: Versioning can never be reversed once enabled, a delete only adds a delete marker so prior versions remain, lifecycle expiration actions delete expired objects on your behalf and NoncurrentVersionExpiration clears old versions (every version is billed in full). Replication requires versioning on both ends and replicates deletions, so it is not a backup; encryption state is irrelevant to expiry and encrypted objects stay encrypted; One Zone-IA uses one AZ, not two.

questions.question: Data-lake objects have an unknown and changing access pattern, and the team refuses to pay per-gigabyte retrieval fees. Which S3 storage class fits?
options: S3 Standard-IA, because infrequent access is always cheaper
S3 Glacier Deep Archive, because it is the cheapest class overall
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which moves objects automatically and charges no retrieval fees
S3 One Zone-IA, because one Availability Zone reduces cost without affecting durability
questions.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering is designed for unknown or changing patterns: objects move to Infrequent Access after 30 days and to Archive Instant after 90 days, with no retrieval fees and only a small per-object monitoring charge. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA both charge retrieval fees and both require a 30-day minimum storage duration; Deep Archive is the cheapest but requires up to hours to restore; and One Zone-IA keeps 11-nines durability while dropping availability to 99.5% by using a single AZ.

questions.question: A marketing team wants to publish a static brochure site from Amazon S3 and asks an architect to confirm the defaults, the public-access posture and the HTTPS story. Which statements are accurate?
options: An S3 static website needs an index document, Block Public Access turned off and a public-read s3:GetObject grant
S3 static websites serve only HTTP endpoints, so HTTPS requires a CDN such as Amazon CloudFront
SSE-S3 has been the default encryption configuration for every bucket since 5 January 2023 at no extra charge
A new bucket starts open to the internet, because public access is an opt-out setting
SSE-KMS reuses the S3 default key, so it never adds a key charge
The bucket Region can be changed later, because only the bucket name is global
questions.explanation: All three keyed statements come straight from the storage dossier: a static website requires an index document plus Block Public Access off and a public-read s3:GetObject grant; static websites support only HTTP endpoints, so HTTPS needs CloudFront in front; and SSE-S3 has encrypted every new object by default since 5 January 2023 at no extra cost. The open-by-default option reverses the real posture, because a bucket is private by default with Block Public Access on and ACLs off. The SSE-KMS option is numeric bait: SSE-KMS adds per-key cost, SSE-C brings your own key, and only SSE-S3 is free. The Region option fails because a bucket Region is fixed at creation even though the globally unique name suggests otherwise, which is why the exam's Region choice comes before the bucket is created.

questions.question: Match each file requirement to the AWS service that satisfies it: the file and gateway answers this exam expects:
prompts: Lift and shift a Windows file server with AD and NTFS permissions
One NFS file system mounted by hundreds of Linux containers
NFS and SMB from a single engine for a mixed protocol team
An on-premises share whose saved files land as S3 objects
A virtual tape library that archives to Glacier over time
options: Amazon EFS
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon S3 File Gateway
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP
AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway
questions.explanation: Each prompt carries the qualifier that picks its service: Windows with Active Directory and NTFS ACLs is FSx for Windows File Server; a POSIX NFS file system shared by many Linux containers is Amazon EFS, which is Regional across at least three Availability Zones; NFS plus SMB from one engine is FSx for NetApp ONTAP; a local share whose files become S3 objects with the path as the key is the S3 File Gateway; and a virtual tape library archiving into Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive is the Tape Gateway. The traps are layer and scope errors: Amazon EFS is not supported with Microsoft Windows, so it cannot answer the lift-and-shift prompt, and FSx for Lustre is on the out-of-scope list, so no option may credit it even though it is a real FSx engine.

questions.question: Two sourced 2025 price changes touch this lesson: effective 10 April 2025, Amazon S3 Express One Zone storage fell 31% (0.16 USD to 0.11 USD per GB-month in us-east-1) with GET requests down 85%; on 5 June 2025, Amazon EC2 NVIDIA GPU instance prices fell by up to 45%. Which statement about these changes is correct?
options: Both are price-only changes: S3 Express One Zone is still a single-AZ, single-digit-millisecond class, and the GPU instances are still accelerated-compute P-family capacity: neither redesign changed what each one is for
The Express One Zone price cut also promoted it to a three-AZ class with S3 Standard's availability profile
The GPU price cut moved those instances to Spot-only capacity, so On-Demand no longer applies to them
Both changes became effective in 2026, so they post-date every fact printed in this lesson's storage-class and instance-family tables
questions.explanation: AWS's 10 April 2025 announcement (What's New plus the AWS News Blog item Up to 85% price reductions for Amazon S3 Express One Zone) cut storage, PUT, GET and upload/retrieval prices in us-east-1 and changed nothing about the class itself: one Availability Zone, single-digit-millisecond latency. The 5 June 2025 announcement cut On-Demand rates by up to 45% (P4d/P4de -33%, P5 -44%, P5en -25%) without altering the instances' role as accelerated-compute capacity. Express One Zone never gained a second AZ, the GPU instances stayed purchasable On-Demand, and both announcements are dated 2025: as of Oct 2026, verify current prices before use.

questions.question: A branch office needs an on-premises iSCSI volume whose hot working set stays local while the complete copy lives in Amazon S3. Which option matches that cached design?
options: Volume Gateway in cached mode: an iSCSI volume with a hot subset kept locally and the data in Amazon S3
Volume Gateway in stored mode: the local primary copy with only asynchronous snapshots sent to Amazon S3
An Amazon EBS volume attached to the on-premises server across the VPN connection
Amazon EFS mounted from the branch office over the public internet link
questions.explanation: The storage lesson describes Volume Gateway cached mode as an iSCSI volume with the data in Amazon S3 and a hot subset retained locally, which is exactly the branch office requirement, and the guide files Storage Gateway as the cached file systems answer. Stored mode reverses the design: the local primary copy is the source and asynchronous snapshots go to S3, so it fails the hot-subset wording. An Amazon EBS volume is scoped to an Availability Zone and attached to an instance inside AWS, so it cannot be an on-premises iSCSI target over a VPN. Amazon EFS is a Regional NFS file system served to AWS workloads such as EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda and Fargate, not a block device for a branch server.

questions.question: A studio wants to store one 55 TB render as a single Amazon S3 object. Which statement about the Amazon S3 object-size ceiling is accurate?
options: A single PUT call uploads up to 50 TB, so one API call can carry the whole render
A single object is capped at 5 TB, so the render must be split into at least 11 parts before upload
A single object is capped at 50 TB, a ceiling raised from 5 TB on 2 December 2025, so 55 TB still exceeds it
Amazon S3 objects have no size ceiling, so the render can be written to the bucket as it stands
questions.explanation: The storage dossier records the raised limit: maximum object size is 50 TB, raised from 5 TB on 2 December 2025, so a 55 TB file still does not fit as one object. The 5 TB figure is the stale pre-December 2025 ceiling, and its split arithmetic answers a question nobody asked. A single PUT carries 5 GB, not 50 TB, so one API call can never carry the render and multipart handling is required for large uploads. Objects do have a size ceiling, so the unlimited option contradicts the same documented limit.

questions.question: A finance analyst reviews a proposed lifecycle rule for a bucket and asks which published storage-class behaviours it may rely on. Which statements are accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: S3 Standard charges no retrieval fee and sets no minimum storage duration
S3 Intelligent-Tiering charges a small per-object monitoring fee, no retrieval fee, and never auto-tiers objects below 128 KB
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval serves free bulk retrievals that complete in 5 to 12 hours
S3 Standard-IA includes retrieval at no extra charge because its storage price already covers it
S3 One Zone-IA keeps objects across at least three Availability Zones like S3 Standard does
S3 Glacier Deep Archive returns objects in minutes as soon as a restore is requested
questions.explanation: The dossier's storage-class lineup confirms the first three: S3 Standard is the default class with no retrieval fee and no minimum storage duration; Intelligent-Tiering charges a monitoring fee of 0.0000025 US dollars per object per month, charges no retrieval fee, and never auto-tiers objects below the 128 KB minimum billable size; and Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers free bulk retrievals that complete in 5 to 12 hours. Standard-IA charges a retrieval fee per GB on top of a 30-day minimum storage duration, so its price does not absorb retrieval. One Zone-IA stores in one Availability Zone with 99.5 percent availability rather than at least three AZs. Deep Archive takes hours to restore, about 12 or 48 hours, behind a 180-day minimum storage duration.

questions.question: Match each backup governance need to the AWS Backup element the storage lesson names for it:
prompts: Selects what to protect on a schedule, usually matched by tag
Holds the KMS-encrypted copies that the plan produces
Makes a stored copy immutable, so it cannot be altered or deleted
Produces the compliance evidence that auditors ask for
Protects EC2, S3, EFS, RDS and DynamoDB under one policy
options: AWS Backup Audit Manager, which reports on backup activity
AWS Backup Vault Lock, which adds write-once-read-many protection
AWS Backup plans, which are policy-driven and tag aware
AWS Backup vaults, the KMS-encrypted destination for copies
AWS Backup itself, the cross-service backup service
questions.explanation: The storage lesson's AWS Backup section names each element: plans select resources, typically by tag, on a schedule; vaults hold the KMS-encrypted copies; AWS Backup Vault Lock provides write-once-read-many protection; AWS Backup Audit Manager reports on backup activity; and one service covers EC2 and EBS, Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB and Storage Gateway volumes. Two plausible readings fail: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager is on the out-of-scope list, so the credited governance answer is always AWS Backup; and AWS Backup does not govern backups you take outside of AWS Backup, so existing native snapshots are never covered automatically. AWS Backup is also additive, carrying extra cost on top of native snapshots rather than replacing their price.

questions.question: A support team wants the sentiment and key phrases of thousands of free-text tickets, with no ML experience. Which in-scope service fits?
options: Amazon Comprehend, a natural language processing service that finds sentiment, entities and PII in text
Amazon SageMaker AI, because every ML task requires building a model
Amazon Textract, because the tickets contain unstructured text
Amazon Rekognition, because it analyses support content
questions.explanation: Comprehend is the NLP service for sentiment, entities, key phrases and PII in text: no ML expertise required. Rekognition handles images and video, Textract extracts text, handwriting and data from scanned documents, and SageMaker AI is for building, training and deploying your own models rather than calling a pre-trained API.

questions.question: Analysts need ad-hoc ANSI SQL directly over objects in Amazon S3, with cost proportional to the data actually read. Which service and cost driver apply?
options: Amazon Quick Sight at 3 USD per user per month for each analyst
Amazon EMR at a per-second rate with a one-minute minimum
AWS Glue at 0.44 USD per DPU-hour, because SQL over S3 requires an ETL cluster
Amazon Athena at 5.00 USD per terabyte scanned, with a 10 MB minimum per query
questions.explanation: Athena is serverless ANSI SQL over S3 priced per query at 5.00 USD per TB of data scanned with a 10 MB minimum, and DDL plus failed queries cost nothing (as of Oct 2026). Glue catalogs and transforms rather than answering SQL, EMR is a cluster you operate, and Quick Sight is the dashboard layer on top: none of them bills by data scanned.

questions.question: A media company needs labels for uploaded photos, a chatbot on its support site, and an in-house model that forecasts churn from its own transaction history. Which statements are accurate?
options: Amazon Rekognition labels and detects objects in the uploaded images and video
Amazon Lex builds the conversational interface and is the technology that powers Amazon Connect
The churn forecast should call a pre-trained API instead of training a model
Amazon SageMaker AI is where the team builds, trains and deploys its own model
Amazon Q is the service chosen to build a custom forecasting model from company data
Amazon Textract labels objects in the uploaded video frames
questions.explanation: The dossier's ML tiering rule decides every option: images go to Rekognition (computer vision), the chatbot goes to Lex (conversational interfaces, and the same technology behind Amazon Connect), and a model built from the company's own data goes to Amazon SageMaker AI, whose AWS wording is build, train and deploy ML models. The pre-trained-API option inverts the rule for this third need, because a custom forecast on proprietary data is the build-your-own case, while the pre-trained tier covers Rekognition, Comprehend, Textract, Transcribe, Translate, Polly and Lex. Amazon Q is generative-AI assistants (Q Business and Q Developer), not a modeller, so it cannot own the churn model. Textract extracts text, handwriting and data from scanned documents; it never labels video frames.

questions.question: A product team is building a serverless analytics path for clickstream records, from the moment the application writes a line to the moment an executive sees a chart. Put the documented pipeline in order and drop the step that does not belong:
options: AWS Glue crawlers catalog the landed objects as tables
Amazon EMR provisions a Hadoop cluster to clean the raw records
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams receives the ordered event log
Amazon Athena runs SQL over the cataloged tables
Amazon Data Firehose batches records and writes them to Amazon S3
Amazon Quick Sight builds the executive dashboard
questions.explanation: The documented serverless analytics pipeline is: records are produced, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams receives them in ordered shards, Amazon Data Firehose batches and writes them to Amazon S3 with no consumer code to write, an AWS Glue crawler catalogs the objects as tables, Amazon Athena runs ANSI SQL over that cataloged data, and Amazon Quick Sight draws the dashboard. Amazon EMR is the step that does not belong: it is a managed Hadoop, Spark, Hive and Presto cluster you operate for big-data processing, and it is not part of this documented chain, so leaving it out is what the ordering tests. Skipping the Glue step is the classic failure, because Athena can only query tables it can see and the Glue Data Catalog is how it sees them, while Glue itself never answers a query.

questions.question: Match each language, speech or document task to the pre-trained AI service that performs it, with no model training:
prompts: Pull text, handwriting and form fields out of scanned pages
Turn a recorded podcast into timestamped written text
Narrate a training video in a lifelike synthetic voice
Localise the help centre into other languages on demand
Flag entities and sensitive details inside chat transcripts
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Translate
Amazon Textract
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Polly
questions.explanation: Each prompt names its data type, and the dossier's rule is never to swap the data type: scanned pages with handwriting and form fields go to Amazon Textract; audio to written text goes to Amazon Transcribe; written text to lifelike speech goes to Amazon Polly; on-demand translation between languages goes to Amazon Translate; and sentiment, entities, key phrases and PII in text go to Amazon Comprehend. The near-misses fail on the same axis: Comprehend cannot read a scanned page's layout, Textract does not listen to audio, and Transcribe produces text rather than speech, so it cannot narrate the video. All five are in-scope purpose-built AI services you call with your data, which is exactly why no SageMaker AI model appears in this list.

questions.question: Employees need answers drawn from internal documentation and developers need an assistant inside their tools, with no model training. Which in-scope machine learning answer covers both needs?
options: Amazon SageMaker AI, because a generative assistant must be built, trained and deployed by the team
Amazon Lex, because every conversational interface in AWS is created with Lex
Amazon Q, whose in-scope generative-AI assistants are Amazon Q Business and Amazon Q Developer
Amazon Kendra, because enterprise search was added to the in-scope machine learning row in 2026
questions.explanation: The tiering rule in the analytics lesson sends a generative-AI assistant for employees or developers to Amazon Q, whose in-scope forms are Amazon Q Business and Amazon Q Developer. SageMaker AI loses because it is the build, train and deploy your own model tier, which the stem explicitly rules out with no model training. Lex builds conversational interfaces and chatbots, so it is not the documentation-answer service either, and it cannot be the only conversational interface in AWS. The Kendra option reverses the recorded 2026 change to the machine learning row: Amazon Q was added and Amazon Kendra was removed from the in-scope list, so it can appear only as a distractor.

questions.question: A growth team wants a managed search and analytics domain where analysts explore clickstream and log data and assemble their own dashboards. Which service is the documented fit?
options: Amazon Athena, which runs ANSI SQL over data already held in Amazon S3
Amazon Redshift, the petabyte warehouse built for complex joins and BI
Amazon CloudWatch, because it already ingests the application logs
Amazon OpenSearch Service, which provides managed domains for log analytics, real-time application monitoring and clickstream analysis plus OpenSearch Dashboards
questions.explanation: The analytics lesson defines Amazon OpenSearch Service as managed domains, which is to say clusters, for log analytics, real-time application monitoring and clickstream analysis, plus search and OpenSearch Dashboards, the Kibana successor; the service was renamed from Amazon Elasticsearch Service on 8 September 2021. CloudWatch is the sibling trap: it is the monitoring family of metrics, alarms, dashboards and Logs that answers is my stuff working, and although CloudWatch Logs Insights searches log groups interactively it never hosts a searchable clickstream domain. Athena answers SQL questions over data in Amazon S3 and bills per terabyte scanned, so it serves queries rather than a search domain. Redshift is the persistent petabyte warehouse chosen for complex joins across very large tables, not an exploration domain.

questions.question: A platform team is sizing Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for a clickstream feed and records five claims about shards, retention and throughput. Which statements are accurate as documented?
options: One shard accepts 1 MB/s of writes and 1,000 records per second, and serves 2 MB/s of reads
Retention is 24 hours by default and can be extended to 365 days, which is what makes replay possible
4,000 records per second averaging 10 KB each need 40 shards on bandwidth and 40 shards on record rate
Amazon Data Firehose exposes shards you size yourself, so its consumers can replay any window
The service writes the consumer code for you, because no consumer library work is needed
A single shard serves 4 MB/s of reads, doubling the documented read limit of a shard
questions.explanation: All three keyed statements are the lesson's shard facts: one shard takes 1 MB/s and 1,000 records per second of writes and serves 2 MB/s of reads; retention is 24 hours by default and up to 365 days, which is what makes replay possible; and the worked example gives 4,000 records per second at 10 KB as 40,000 KB/s, that is 40 MB/s, so bandwidth yields 40 shards and record rate yields 40 shards, with both constraints agreeing. Amazon Data Firehose is the sibling service that fails twice: it has no shards to size and no replay window, because it batches in near real time with no consumer code to write. Kinesis inverts that last point instead - you write the consumer code yourself - and the documented read limit is 2 MB/s per shard, not 4 MB/s.

questions.question: Survey exports already sit in an Amazon S3 bucket and analysts want SQL answers plus a chart. Arrange the steps of the working sequence and leave out the element that does not belong:
options: A Glue crawler writes table definitions into the Glue Data Catalog
An Amazon Redshift warehouse is loaded before the first question is asked
Amazon Athena answers the analysts' questions with ANSI SQL
The survey exports arrive in an Amazon S3 bucket
Amazon Quick Sight renders the chart from the query results
questions.explanation: The documented path is land, catalog, query, present: the exports land in Amazon S3, an AWS Glue crawler writes table definitions into the Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena runs ANSI SQL over that cataloged data at 5.00 US dollars per terabyte scanned with a 10 MB minimum, and Amazon Quick Sight draws the dashboard. Skipping the catalog step is the classic mistake, because Athena can only query tables it can see and the Glue Data Catalog is how it sees them. The Redshift step does not belong: Athena is serverless with no cluster to launch, so nothing must be loaded into a warehouse before the first question, and Redshift is chosen instead for lots of joins across lots of very large tables in a persistent warehouse.

questions.question: An analytics team keeps mixing up five services. For each workload below, name the service that the analytics lesson actually documents:
prompts: Run open-source Spark and Hive on clusters billed per second
Answer complex joins over very large tables in a petabyte warehouse
Build, train and deploy a custom model in a hosted environment
Serve BI dashboards from the SPICE in-memory engine
Run ANSI SQL over Amazon S3 at 5.00 USD per terabyte scanned
options: Amazon Quick Sight
Amazon Athena
Amazon EMR
Amazon SageMaker AI
Amazon Redshift
questions.explanation: Each prompt is a tie-breaker from the analytics lesson: Amazon EMR is managed Hadoop, Spark, Hive and Presto clusters on EC2 billed per second with a one-minute minimum on top of EC2, EBS and the EMR uplift, with no flat standalone EMR fee; Amazon Redshift is the managed petabyte-scale columnar warehouse for complex joins and BI; Amazon SageMaker AI is AWS's build, train and deploy ML models into a production-ready hosted environment; Amazon Quick Sight is the BI service where SPICE is the in-memory engine against direct query; and Amazon Athena is serverless ANSI SQL over Amazon S3 at 5.00 US dollars per terabyte scanned with a 10 MB minimum. The swaps fail on layer: Athena launches no cluster, so it cannot run Spark and Hive; Glue catalogs and prepares data instead of answering a query; and Quick Sight renders results rather than training a model.

questions.question: A SaaS vendor's events must trigger a Lambda function only when a specific field matches, and a batch job must run nightly at 02:00 UTC. Which service and which documented limits apply?
options: Amazon SNS, because topics support cron expressions and up to five subscriptions
AWS Step Functions, because one state can wait until 02:00 UTC
Amazon SQS, because long polling can wait up to 20 seconds for a schedule
Amazon EventBridge: a rule can have up to five targets, there are up to 300 rules per event bus, and scheduled rules are handled by EventBridge Scheduler
questions.explanation: Content-filtered JSON events, SaaS partner sources and schedules are EventBridge's job: a single rule can send an event to up to five targets, an event bus holds up to 300 rules, and AWS steers scheduled rules to EventBridge Scheduler with 14,000,000 free invocations per month. SNS has no cron, Step Functions is for multi-step processes, and SQS long polling is a 20-second receive wait, not a scheduler.

questions.question: A developer claims a standard Amazon SQS queue processes every message exactly once, in the order it was sent. Which correction is accurate?
options: Standard queues give at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering, while FIFO queues give exactly-once processing with strict FIFO order
Both queue types guarantee exactly-once delivery; FIFO only adds strict ordering
Standard queues are exactly-once and FIFO queues are at-least-once
Both types are best-effort and ordering is always the caller's responsibility
questions.explanation: AWS documents standard queues as at-least-once delivery where a message may be delivered more than once, with best-effort ordering, and FIFO queues as exactly-once processing with strict order plus a 5-minute deduplication interval. Duplicates on standard queues are expected, so consumers must be idempotent.

questions.question: A company must present the output of its virtual machines on staff laptops and tablets without shipping hardware, and it wants a browser-only option for contractors. Which statements are accurate?
options: Amazon WorkSpaces delivers fully managed persistent virtual desktops to end users
Amazon AppStream 2.0 streams desktop applications to any browser or device without rewriting code
Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser keeps HTML and document object model data off the local machine
AWS Amplify presents virtual desktop sessions inside a browser tab
Amazon WorkDocs supplies the in-scope virtual desktop for the contractors
Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser transmits the document object model to the user device
questions.explanation: The end-user-computing stem in the dossier is verbatim: the services that present the output of virtual machines on end-user machines are Amazon AppStream 2.0 for applications, Amazon WorkSpaces for full desktops, and Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser for browser only, and that hosted browser transmits no HTML, document object model or sensitive company data to the local machine. AWS Amplify fails on category: it creates and deploys frontend web and mobile applications, so it builds the client rather than presenting a virtual machine. Amazon WorkDocs fails on category: it was a document collaboration and file-sharing service, never a desktop delivery service, so it cannot supply the virtual desktop the option promises. The last option is a straight contradiction of the Secure Browser guarantee, which is the claim the exam tests when a stem mentions contractor access.

questions.question: A warehouse team wants a StockUnavailable line in its application log to become a notification to the on-call channel. Order the documented chain from the log line to the delivered message and ignore the step that is not part of it:
options: An Amazon SNS topic delivers the notification to subscribers
AWS Health reports a service disruption in the Region
A CloudWatch alarm evaluates the metric and changes state
A log event arrives in the CloudWatch Logs group
A metric filter counts matching log lines and emits a metric
questions.explanation: The dossier documents the chain as log event, metric filter, alarm, then SNS action: the line lands in a CloudWatch Logs group, a metric filter turns matching lines into a metric such as OutOfStockError, the alarm evaluates that metric and changes state, and the alarm action publishes to an Amazon SNS topic that reaches email, SMS, HTTP or Lambda subscribers. AWS Health is the step that does not belong, because it answers is AWS's stuff working rather than is my application working, so it never sits inside your own log-to-notification path. Order matters too: the alarm cannot evaluate a metric the filter has not yet emitted, and the SNS topic is only reached after the alarm acts, which is why actions fire on state change rather than on every breaching minute.

questions.question: Match each delivery or diagnostic need to the in-scope service that answers it, using the 2026 task 3.8 categories:
prompts: Compile source code and run unit tests in the build stage
Trace a request across microservices for 30 days
Hold a workflow that waits three days for human approval
Build and deploy a frontend web or mobile application
Connect field devices that speak MQTT or HTTP to the cloud
options: AWS X-Ray
AWS Amplify
AWS CodeBuild
AWS IoT Core
AWS Step Functions
questions.explanation: Each prompt maps to one documented task 3.8 answer: AWS CodeBuild compiles your source code, runs unit tests and produces artifacts, billed per build minute with 100 free minutes per month; AWS X-Ray is distributed tracing, segments to traces to a service graph, with trace data retained 30 days; AWS Step Functions Standard runs up to one year with exactly-once execution, which is what a three-day human approval wait needs; AWS Amplify creates and deploys frontend web and mobile applications; and AWS IoT Core is the managed gateway that connects devices over MQTT or HTTP. The plausible alternatives fail on layer: an Amazon SQS delay tops out at 15 minutes and a three-day wait is not a queue's job, AWS CodePipeline models the release stages rather than compiling code, and Amazon WorkSpaces presents desktops instead of connecting devices. Also note the 2026 Developer Tools row holds only AWS CLI, AWS CodeBuild, AWS CodePipeline and AWS X-Ray, so older rosters naming CodeStar or Cloud9 are superseded.

questions.question: A REST API in one Region suddenly receives 12,000 requests per second. What does Amazon API Gateway do by default?
options: It queues every request indefinitely and all of them succeed
It deletes the API once the 5,000-request burst bucket is emptied
It scales without limit and adds a surcharge above 10,000 RPS
It throttles against a default of 10,000 RPS plus a 5,000-request burst per account per Region, returning HTTP 429 Too Many Requests to excess calls: documented as best-effort, not a hard limit
questions.explanation: Default throttling is per account per Region at 10,000 RPS with an additional 5,000-request burst capacity; requests beyond it receive 429 Too Many Requests, and AWS states these are not hard limits and are applied on a best-effort basis. Nothing is queued indefinitely, the API is never deleted, and there is no automatic surcharge above the throttle.

questions.question: One alarm must notify an email address, an SMS number, and three independent consumer services that each retry on their own schedule. Which design is correct?
options: Publish once to an Amazon SNS topic with five subscriptions: email, SMS and three SQS queues: so each subscriber retries independently
Use Amazon SES to send the alert to all five destinations
Write the alarm to a single Amazon SQS queue and let all five consumers read that queue
Publish to Amazon EventBridge and have each destination poll the event bus
questions.explanation: SNS is the push pub/sub service whose subscriptions include email, SMS, HTTP/S, Lambda and SQS; one publish fans out a copy to every subscription, and an SQS queue behind each consumer family gives it an independent backlog and retry policy. A single SQS queue forces competing consumers, EventBridge does not deliver to email or SMS, and SES is email only.

questions.question: A subscription business must send transactional email from its billing application, staff a cloud contact centre, and answer common questions with a bot. Which statements are accurate?
options: Amazon SES sends scalable transactional, marketing and mass email from within any application over API or SMTP
Amazon Connect is a cloud contact centre covering voice, chat and tasks with intelligent routing and real-time agent tracking
Amazon Connect bills only for usage, with no per-seat licence fee
Amazon SNS should carry the marketing email blasts, because its topics deliver to email subscribers
Amazon Lex is the full contact centre, because a chatbot builder also runs voice queues and agent dashboards
AWS Amplify presents the contact centre agents' desktop sessions inside a browser tab
questions.explanation: Task 3.8's business applications row answers all three: Amazon SES is scalable email from within any application - transactional, marketing and mass mail - sent via API or SMTP; Amazon Connect is the cloud contact centre for voice, chat and tasks with intelligent routing and real-time agent performance tracking; and Connect charges only for usage with no per-seat fee. Amazon SNS is the push pub/sub fan-out for notifications, while the lesson's stem split sends email at scale to Amazon SES, so a topic of email subscriptions is the wrong tool for a marketing blast. Lex builds conversational interfaces and is the technology that powers Amazon Connect, which makes it a component rather than the contact centre itself. AWS Amplify creates and deploys frontend web and mobile applications, so it builds clients instead of presenting virtual machine output, a job that belongs to Amazon AppStream 2.0 or Amazon WorkSpaces.

questions.question: A payments service must trace how one message travels through a standard Amazon SQS queue, including what happens when a consumer fails. Order the documented sequence and ignore the step that does not belong:
options: An Amazon SNS topic fans the message out, because a queue cannot receive from a producer
A consumer receives the message through long polling and the message turns invisible to other consumers
A producer writes the message and the queue persists it as a store-and-forward buffer
A consumer that cannot finish leaves the message visible again after the 30-second visibility timeout
A dead-letter queue holds the messages that repeatedly fail
questions.explanation: The lesson documents Amazon SQS as a pull-based, store-and-forward buffer: the producer writes and the queue persists the message, a consumer receives it through long polling, and the message becomes invisible to other consumers for the visibility timeout, which defaults to 30 seconds within a 0 to 12 hour range. A consumer that never deletes the message leaves it visible again after those 30 seconds, which is exactly why duplicates are normal on standard queues, and messages that repeatedly fail are held in a dead-letter queue for later diagnosis. The SNS step does not belong: a producer writes to its own queue directly, and push fan-out to many subscribers is the separate SNS pattern rather than a prerequisite for any queue.

questions.question: A release team has five jobs and five candidate services. Pair each job with the in-scope service that performs it:
prompts: Store and version the container images that ECS or EKS tasks pull
Run containers with no cluster instances to provision or patch
Model and run the stages of a release workflow
Issue AWS API calls from a shell step inside a build
Find, buy and deploy third-party software on one bill
options: AWS CodePipeline, the managed release workflow
AWS CLI, the open source command-line tool
Amazon ECR, the managed container image registry
AWS Marketplace, a curated digital catalog
AWS Fargate, the serverless compute engine for containers
questions.explanation: The task 3.8 categories decide every pair: Amazon ECR is an AWS managed container image registry service, so images are stored and versioned there; AWS Fargate is the serverless compute engine for containers that works with both Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, billed per vCPU and per GB of memory per second with a one-minute minimum, so nothing is provisioned or patched; AWS CodePipeline is the managed release workflow that models the steps and runs the stages; AWS CLI is the open source tool that runs commands in your command-line shell; and AWS Marketplace is the curated digital catalog to find, buy, deploy and manage third-party software on one bill. Two near misses fail on role: AWS CodeBuild compiles source code and runs unit tests inside a stage rather than modelling the workflow, and ECR stores images instead of orchestrating anything, so an option that makes ECR sound like an orchestrator is the trap the compute lesson already flags.

questions.question: A team stops their Amazon RDS database every night to save money, but the bill barely moves. Which statement explains the remaining charges?
options: Stopped RDS instances are billed for provisioned storage and backup storage: only DB instance hours stop
RDS bills a 10-minute minimum for every stop and start operation performed
RDS converts the instance to Spot pricing while stopped, which is not cheaper
Backup storage is free for the first 12 months regardless of account age
questions.explanation: AWS states that while a database instance is stopped you are charged for provisioned storage and backup storage, but not for DB instance hours. Instance billing runs in 1-second increments with a 10-minute minimum while running, but that minimum is not what generates the stopped-instance charge: and longer backup retention simply increases it.

questions.question: Which combination gives BOTH a discount and a guaranteed capacity reservation in a specific Availability Zone?
options: A Compute Savings Plan plus an On-Demand instance
An On-Demand Capacity Reservation purchased at a discounted rate
A Standard Reserved Instance scoped to a specific Availability Zone
A Spot Instance fleet spread across three Availability Zones
questions.explanation: Only an AZ-scoped Standard Reserved Instance delivers both: the discount (up to 72% as of Oct 2026) and the capacity reservation. Savings Plans reserve nothing; an On-Demand Capacity Reservation reserves AZ capacity but bills at the full On-Demand price with no discount; Spot capacity can be reclaimed at any time.

questions.question: Which statement BEST captures AWS's general pricing principles in AWS's own sequence?
options: Pay a fixed annual contract, then negotiate volume rebates annually
Pay as you go, pay for what you use, pay less as you use more, and pay even less when you reserve capacity
Pay upfront for all capacity, then receive credits for unused hours
Pay per user seat, with discounts applied only by enterprise agreement
questions.explanation: AWS's How AWS Pricing Works whitepaper (published 24 February 2023) states exactly that sequence, and the live pricing page adds that pay-as-you-go works 'without requiring long-term contracts'. The three cost drivers are compute, storage and outbound data transfer, with inbound transfer free of charge.

questions.question: A platform team is forecasting egress for a new media pipeline, and its finance lead asks which statements about AWS data-transfer billing hold true as of October 2026. Which statements are correct?
options: Data transferred into AWS from the internet is free of charge
The free outbound allowance is granted separately to every AWS Region
Traffic between two services inside one Availability Zone costs nothing
Data transferred out to the internet is billed at one flat rate
Inter-Region outbound transfer draws on its own separate free allowance
questions.explanation: Inbound transfer from the internet is never charged, and traffic between services in the same Availability Zone is free, so those two statements are the correct pair. The outbound allowance is 100 GB per month aggregated across all AWS services and all Regions (excluding the China Regions and GovCloud), not granted per Region, so the second option is numeric bait (T6) on a true figure. Outbound transfer is tiered per GB - us-east-1 steps down as monthly volume rises - so the flat-rate option fails on structure, and Inter-Region outbound transfer is billed per GB out of that same global allowance rather than a second free pool.

questions.question: A team must choose an EC2 purchase option for several unrelated workloads and decides to walk AWS's purchase-option decision tree. Put the tree's branches in the order the tree visits them.
options: Steady and predictable workloads committed for one or three years
A temporary lab, a course exercise or a first prototype
Guaranteed launch room in a single Availability Zone
Fault-tolerant work that can be interrupted safely
Everything else with an unknown or short-lived pattern
questions.explanation: The tree opens with the free, no-risk branch: a temporary lab, learning exercise or first prototype goes to the Free Tier, which never answers a production-workload question. Next comes fault-tolerant, interruptible work, which is Spot (repriced about every 5 minutes, up to 90 percent off). Only then does it consider a steady, predictable workload needing a 1- or 3-year commitment: Standard Reserved Instance or EC2 Instance Savings Plan up to 72 percent, Compute Savings Plan or Convertible RI up to 66 percent. Guaranteed room in a single Availability Zone sits after the discount decision because an On-Demand Capacity Reservation grants no discount and bills whether the capacity is used or not; everything left over falls to On-Demand, the baseline with zero percent discount. The plausible wrong order - buying the deepest-discount commitment first - fails because the tree clears the free and interruptible options before any multi-year commitment.

questions.question: Match each monthly billing pattern an S3 or RDS owner reports to the charge dimension that explains it:
prompts: Bytes held in an S3 storage class during the month
A PUT request sent to an S3 bucket
Objects pulled back from an infrequent-access class
An Amazon RDS instance switched off for the month
options: Requests per 1,000; DELETE and CANCEL are free
Only instance hours stop; storage keeps billing
Storage in GB-month, priced by storage class
Retrieval per GB plus a minimum storage duration
questions.explanation: Every S3 storage class bills in GB-month at its own monthly rate, so stored bytes match the storage dimension. A PUT is a request charge counted per 1,000 requests, and DELETE and CANCEL requests are free while LIST bills at the PUT rate, so the PUT matches the request dimension. Reading data back out of an infrequent-access or archive class adds a per-GB retrieval charge plus a minimum storage duration, so retrieval is the third match. The stopped RDS instance is the trap: only DB instance hours stop, while provisioned storage and backup storage keep billing - and a stopped EC2 instance is no different, because EBS volumes, snapshots and data transfer continue. The second plausible miss is pricing GET at the PUT rate: GET and HEAD are far cheaper than PUT, COPY, POST and LIST.

questions.question: A finance team asks which commitment discount applies to its Amazon RDS and Amazon DynamoDB workloads, and quotes a December 2025 announcement about Database Savings Plans offering up to 35% off a 1-year, no-upfront commitment. Which statement is correct for CLF-C02 as of Oct 2026?
options: Database Savings Plans replaced On-Demand billing for every AWS database, so RDS and DynamoDB are no longer billed hourly
Database Savings Plans is named in the CLF-C02 exam guide as a fourth commitment option alongside On-Demand, Reserved Instances and Spot
Database Savings Plans is real and recently launched (up to 35%, 1-year, no upfront), but the guide still names only AWS Savings Plans; so it is news, not an examinable answer
Database Savings Plans applies only to Amazon Aurora and never to DynamoDB or other database engines
questions.explanation: AWS announced Database Savings Plans on 2 December 2025 with savings of up to 35% for a 1-year, no-upfront commitment (serverless up to 35%, provisioned up to 20%, DynamoDB 18%, Amazon Keyspaces 12%) - but the live CLF-C02 guide's task statements still say AWS Savings Plans, and neither Database Savings Plans nor the 2026 Well-Architected Agent appears anywhere in the guide. The exam tests the guide you download today: On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Spot and Savings Plans remain the commitment vocabulary, coverage applies beyond Aurora, and the percentages are dated offers to re-check as of Oct 2026 rather than guarantees.

questions.question: As of Oct 2026, a design runs two NAT gateways for a full 730-hour month in US East (Ohio) at 0.045 USD per hour, processes 500 GB through NAT at 0.045 USD per GB, and sends a further 500 GB to the internet at 0.09 USD per GB. What is the approximate monthly total?
options: 65.70 USD: only the two hourly charges are billed
88.20 USD: hourly charges plus NAT processing, but internet egress is free
110.70 USD: hourly charges plus internet egress, but NAT processing is free
133.20 USD: hourly charges plus NAT processing plus internet data transfer out
questions.explanation: There are three separate charges: 2 x 730 x 0.045 USD = 65.70 USD hourly, 500 x 0.045 USD = 22.50 USD NAT processing, and 500 x 0.09 USD = 45.00 USD internet data transfer out, giving 133.20 USD per month. Options offering a single-charge total are testing whether you noticed that a NAT gateway bills by the hour AND per GB, and that leaving AWS still costs per GB.

questions.question: Using the Lambda pricing components verified for this lesson (as of Oct 2026), what does a month of 2,000,000 invocations at 100 ms and 1,024 MB cost?
options: About 0.20 USD: one million billable requests at 0.20 USD per million, and 200,000 GB-seconds still inside the 400,000 free allowance
About 0.60 USD: all two million requests are billable at 0.20 USD per million
About 2.00 USD: Lambda always bills the listed 1,000 GB-second block
Zero - Lambda is serverless, so it is never billed while a function is running
questions.explanation: Requests: 2,000,000 minus the 1,000,000 Always Free requests leaves 1,000,000 x 0.20 USD per million = 0.20 USD. Duration: 1 GB x 0.1 s = 0.1 GB-s per call, x 2,000,000 = 200,000 GB-s, which is under the 400,000 GB-second monthly allowance, so duration is free. Lambda bills only while code executes: idle costs nothing; but it is absolutely billed per request and per GB-second when it runs.

questions.question: A team is weighing Spot Instances for a nightly batch pipeline and wants only what AWS publishes about Spot behaviour as of October 2026. Which statements are correct?
options: AWS reprices the Spot price about every five minutes
Spot is the only purchase option AWS lists as interruptible
Instance Advisor has historically reported average interruption frequency under 5 percent on a 30-day view as of Oct 2026
Spot requires a one-year or three-year term commitment
Spot is the right choice for a stateful, latency-critical workload
Spot buys the deepest discount while surrendering no availability at all
questions.explanation: AWS reprices the Spot price about every five minutes, Spot is the only interruptible option among the Task 4.1 purchase options, and AWS's Instance Advisor reports an average interruption frequency that has historically stayed under 5 percent on a 30-day view across all Regions and instance types (as of Oct 2026). The traps fail on three different facts: Spot carries no term commitment of any kind, so a one- or three-year term belongs to Reserved Instances and Savings Plans; Spot fits only fault-tolerant, stateless, restartable work such as batch jobs and CI pipelines, never a stateful latency-critical tier; and the deepest discount sits at the opposite end of the axis from availability, because Spot capacity runs only whenever capacity is available and can be reclaimed [source: 13-pricing-models.md 2.1, 2.5].

questions.question: A cost analyst is ranking outbound data transfer rates for US East (N. Virginia) from the 7 October 2026 pricing feed. Put the paid per-GB tiers in the order AWS applies them as monthly volume rises; one option is not a paid per-GB tier.
options: 5 cents per GB, the lowest rate once monthly volume is largest
9 cents per GB, the rate that opens the paid tiers
The 100 GB allowance that AWS grants free each month across all services
7 cents per GB
8.5 cents per GB
questions.explanation: The 7 October 2026 feed for us-east-1 steps outbound transfer down from nine cents per GB to 8.5, then 7, then 5 cents as monthly volume rises, so the paid order is 9, 8.5, 7, 5. The 100 GB option is not a rate at all: it is the free monthly allowance aggregated across all AWS services and all Regions (excluding the China Regions and AWS GovCloud), it is granted per month rather than per service or per Region, and placing it inside the tier ladder would be numeric bait (T6) on a true figure. Transfer IN from the internet stays free of charge, which is why only outbound rates appear in this ranking at all [source: 13-pricing-models.md 1.2, 4.4].

questions.question: Match each pricing fact a team re-verifies to the number or rule AWS published, using the worked feed of 7 October 2026 and the current guide:
prompts: The 7 Oct 2026 feed for t3.medium on Linux in Sao Paulo
The same t3.medium feed for US East (N. Virginia)
What a Local Zone bills compared with its parent Region
Free capacity CloudFront adds each month above the 100 GB pool
The guide note AWS cites for the price gap between Regions
options: Priced higher than its parent Region
About 4.16 cents per hour, about 30.37 USD for 730 hours
1 TB of data transfer out plus 10,000,000 HTTP(S) requests
About 6.72 cents per hour, about 49.06 USD for 730 hours
COST07-BP02: resource pricing may be different in each Region
questions.explanation: Prices are set per service AND per Region, and the 7 October 2026 worked feed for t3.medium on Linux reads 4.16 cents per hour in US East (N. Virginia) against 6.72 cents in Sao Paulo, about 61 percent dearer, which over 730 hours is about 30.37 versus 49.06 USD. Local Zones are priced higher than their parent Region, and the guide's cost-optimisation note COST07-BP02 explains the gap with land, fiber, electricity and taxes. Amazon CloudFront separately adds 1 TB of free data transfer out plus 10,000,000 free HTTP(S) requests per month, and the lesson warns against labelling that allowance Always Free or 12-month without re-checking. The traps: swapping the two feeds reverses which Region is dearer, and quoting a Regional price without its date and Region is exactly how stale figures survive (verify current before use) [source: 13-pricing-models.md 1.2, 1.4, 3.1; 01-exam-guide-cloud-concepts.md 9.3].

questions.question: Requirement: notify the finance channel at 80% of a 50,000 USD monthly budget AND automatically prevent the creation of additional resources if the budget is breached. Which combination satisfies it?
options: AWS Cost Explorer with a forecast alert and an SNS topic
AWS Budgets with a threshold notification plus a budget action that applies an IAM policy denying provisioning
An SCP alone, because SCPs cap spending
The Cost and Usage Report delivered daily to S3
questions.explanation: AWS's documented pattern is to notify at 80 percent of the budgeted amount and apply an action: for example a custom IAM policy that denies provisioning additional resources. Budget actions can run programmatically or with approval and can apply IAM policies, SCPs or AWS resources, integrating with AWS Chatbot. Cost Explorer explores and forecasts but never enforces; an SCP can deny provisioning actions yet it cannot watch a spend target or notify anyone; the CUR is only an export.

questions.question: You need the PDF invoice, the tax lines and the issued-versus-pending status of this month's AWS bill. Which page do you open?
options: The Bills page
Payment preferences
AWS Cost Explorer default report
The Billing dashboard Home page
questions.explanation: The Bills page holds the bill summary (Issued vs Pending), payment information, charges by service (drillable to Region), charges by account (management account only), downloadable PDF invoices, savings and taxes. Home is the exploratory widget view, Cost Explorer answers 'why did cost move', and Payment preferences is where you change method or currency.

questions.question: A finance lead asks what actually changes when five subsidiary accounts move under AWS Organizations with consolidated billing. Which statements about that change are correct as of October 2026?
options: AWS treats every account as one account when it applies volume tier thresholds
A Reserved Instance bought by one account can discount other accounts' usage
AWS Marketplace charges land on the same consolidated bill
Support fees are pooled and charged once for the whole organization
Consolidated billing adds a separate monthly fee on top of usage
Each member account reaches volume thresholds on its own bill
questions.explanation: AWS treats all accounts in an organization as a single account, so member accounts do not reach tier thresholds individually - pooling is correct. Consolidated billing shares volume discounts, Reserved Instance discounts and Savings Plans across accounts, so an RI bought by one account can discount another account's usage - correct. AWS Marketplace usage is billed on the same invoice because one bill covers each seller of record - correct. Support is the documented exception: AWS calculates support fees independently for each member account and each account subscribes independently, so pooled support fails. Consolidated billing carries no extra fee as of October 2026, so the surcharge option fails, and the last option is a responsibility flip: it restates pre-consolidation behaviour, since aggregation is per service and every month starts at zero.

questions.question: A cloud finance analyst wants to split last month's shared platform spend between two product teams using a single tag. Put the required steps in the order they must happen.
options: Activate the user-defined tag as a cost allocation tag
Restructure the organizational units so each team is billed separately
Tag every billable resource with one consistent key
Group last month's spend by that tag in Cost Explorer
Wait up to 24 hours for the tag to reach cost data
questions.explanation: The tag must exist on every billable resource first, with one consistent key. Second it is activated as a cost allocation tag - and activation lives in the management account or a standalone account, because member accounts cannot activate tags. Third, allow up to 24 hours for the activated tag to start flowing into cost data. Fourth, group by that tag in Cost Explorer, or read it in the Cost and Usage Report, then reconcile against the Bills page. The restructure option is the trap: AWS states your bill will not reflect the structure you have defined in your organization, so adding or reshaping OUs never splits spend - activated cost allocation tags or cost categories do. Expect an untagged row too: resources tagged after the fact and non-tagging services never appear under the key.

questions.question: Match each cost-management question a team asks to the AWS tool that answers it:
prompts: Estimate a three-tier application before it is built
Send raw hourly line items to a bucket you control
Explain a bill increase, filtered by Region
Alert the team when forecast spend passes a target
Split Marketplace monthly fees that tags cannot cover
options: AWS Cost and Usage Report, daily CSV or Parquet to your bucket
AWS Budgets, notifications by email or Amazon SNS
AWS Pricing Calculator, free and needs no AWS account
AWS Cost Explorer, filter by service, Region and tag
Cost categories, since tags cannot allocate monthly fees
questions.explanation: Estimating an application that does not exist yet is the Pricing Calculator: a free web tool that needs no AWS account, assumes 730 hours in a month and does not assume the Free Tier, while Cost Explorer reads actual usage. Raw hourly line items delivered at least daily to your own S3 bucket in CSV or Parquet is the Cost and Usage Report, which carries both unblended and blended rates. Explaining a movement by Region, service or tag is Cost Explorer, whose console clicks are free (only API calls are billed) and whose data reflects usage up to the previous day. A threshold alert is AWS Budgets: monitoring and notifications are free, but an alert is a notification, not a cap - stopping spend needs a budget action. Finally, subscription-based charges such as AWS Support and AWS Marketplace monthly fees cannot be allocated by tags, so the escape hatch is a cost category.

questions.question: You hold a 10 USD/hour Savings Plans commitment; usage billed with Savings Plans rates totalled 9.80 USD. Separately, 9 of 10 identical 1.00 USD/hour instances ran at Savings Plans rates. What do these two readings indicate?
options: Utilization 98% (slight over-buy risk) and coverage 90% (one instance still On-Demand)
Coverage 98% and utilization 90% - both indicate under-buying
Utilization 98% and coverage 90% - both indicate under-buying
Reservation report shows both numbers; utilization and coverage are the same metric
questions.explanation: Utilization answers 'of the commitment I bought, how much did I use?' - 9.80/10.00 = 98%, so 2% of what you paid for was idle (over-buy signal). Coverage answers 'of the hours I ran, how many were covered?' - 9/10 = 90%, so 10% still runs at On-Demand rates (under-buy signal). They are separate Budgets types and separate Cost Explorer reports, and reports use normalized units so instance sizes compare fairly.

questions.question: As of Oct 2026, three subsidiaries in one AWS organization each store about 31,667 GB of S3 Standard, roughly 95 TB together. What does consolidated billing do to the monthly charge under AWS's published S3 Standard tiers?
options: Combining the three pushes the whole estate into dearer storage tiers, costing about 940 USD more
About 6,720 USD pooled instead of about 7,660 USD billed separately, a saving of about 940 USD or about 12.3 percent
A consolidated billing surcharge of about 12.3 percent cancels the volume saving
No change: each subsidiary climbs the S3 storage price tiers on its own usage
questions.explanation: AWS treats all accounts in an organization as a single account, so member accounts do not reach tier thresholds individually: aggregation happens per service and every month starts at zero. Worked through AWS's published S3 Standard tiers (0.10 USD per GB for the first 1,000 GB, 0.08 USD for the next 49,000 GB, 0.06 USD thereafter, as of Oct 2026, verify current), the three accounts pay about 6,720 USD pooled against about 7,660 USD billed separately, a saving of about 940 USD, about 12.3 percent. The first option states the exact opposite of the pooling rule, because combined usage qualifies for the cheaper bands instead of climbing alone; the second reverses the direction of the saving; and the fourth invents a surcharge, since AWS offers Organizations and consolidated billing at no additional charge [source: 14-billing-organizations.md 2.1, 3.1, 3.2].

questions.question: A team switches on AWS Budgets for the first time and asks what the service supports as of Oct 2026. Which statements are correct?
options: Six budget types exist: Cost, Usage, RI utilization, RI coverage, SP utilization and SP coverage
Reserved Instance and Savings Plans budgets fire when their value falls below a threshold
Monitoring and notifications are free, and a budget without actions costs nothing
The first five action-enabled budgets in a month are free of charge
A notification by itself stops further provisioning as soon as spend crosses the line
Budgets refresh many times an hour, so an alert always lands within minutes
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets offers exactly six budget types, and notifications fire when values exceed or are forecast to exceed the threshold for cost and usage budgets, while Reserved Instance and Savings Plans budgets fire when values fall below it. Monitoring and notifications are free and budgets without actions cost nothing, so a zero-cost budget is a free spend alert. The traps: only the first two action-enabled budgets per month are free and each later one costs ten cents per day (one such budget over a 30-day month is 3 USD); a notification is not a cap, because stopping spend needs a budget action that applies an IAM policy, an SCP or a resource; and budgets refresh at most three times a day, typically 8 to 12 hours apart, so delivery lags the charge instead of landing within minutes [source: 14-billing-organizations.md 7.1; 13-pricing-models.md 5.3].

questions.question: An analyst wants AWS Cost Anomaly Detection to watch spend and alert the team. Put the setup in the order AWS documents for it as of Oct 2026; one option belongs to a different cost tool.
options: Define the cost monitor over the services or dimension to watch
Accumulate at least 10 days of billing history for the account
Apply a budget action that denies provisioning at the threshold
Attach an alert subscription to the monitor
Receive the anomaly alert within 24 hours of detection
questions.explanation: A cost monitor needs at least 10 days of history before it can read a deviation, so history comes first; the documented flow is then cost monitor, alert subscription, notification, with alerts issued within 24 hours. The budget-action option belongs to AWS Budgets, not to anomaly detection: Cost Anomaly Detection is awareness-only and is never the keyed answer when Budgets or Cost Explorer also fits, and it never stops anything, because stopping spend requires a budget action that applies an IAM policy, an SCP or an AWS resource. If the requirement were enforcement rather than detection, AWS Budgets with a threshold notification plus an action would be the answer [source: 14-billing-organizations.md 7.1, 7.5].

questions.question: Match each billing or governance need to the AWS feature or rule that delivers it, as of Oct 2026:
prompts: Apply a service control policy that denies actions in member accounts
Take one bill with pooled volume discounts but without any SCPs
Read a member account's charges before any rate averaging
Why one line shows full On-Demand price while the org total falls
Offer a negotiated price and EULA to a named set of accounts
options: Consolidated billing only, with no tag policies or SCPs
An AWS Marketplace private offer for up to 25 accounts
All features of AWS Organizations, the set that includes SCPs
Unblended costs, which each member account sees
Blended rates computed at the management account
questions.explanation: Service control policies exist only in the all-features set of AWS Organizations, which also brings tag policies and service integrations. The consolidated-billing-only feature set still gives one bill, pooled volume pricing discounts and Reserved Instance and Savings Plans sharing, but no SCPs, no tag policies and no integrations. AWS shows each member account its charges as unblended costs, while blended rates are computed at the management account, so one account's line can read the full On-Demand price while the organization total falls. A negotiated price and EULA for up to 25 named accounts is an AWS Marketplace private offer, which differs from a Private Marketplace: a curated catalog scoped to the whole organization, OUs or accounts that requires the all-features set. Consolidated billing itself adds no extra fee, so none of these options charges for the privilege [source: 14-billing-organizations.md 2.3, 3.1, 3.3, 4.1, 8.1].

questions.question: A customer on the Basic Support plan suffers a production outage and wants to escalate to AWS immediately. Which statement is correct?
options: Basic includes a designated Technical Account Manager
Basic includes the full Trusted Advisor check set, so the case is unnecessary
Basic cannot open technical support cases: it covers billing and account help, quota increases, forums, documentation and service health
Basic includes a first response within 1 hour for production system down
questions.explanation: Customers with the Basic Support plan cannot open technical support cases. What Basic does include, 24x7, is billing and account support, quota increases, forums, documentation and service health: plus Trusted Advisor core checks (all accounts get 56 free checks). Response-time ladders and TAMs only exist on plans that can open technical cases.

questions.question: Which statement about AWS Trusted Advisor availability is correct as of Oct 2026?
options: Customers on the Basic Support plan get no Trusted Advisor checks at all
Business Support+ includes TA Priority as well as the full check set
Trusted Advisor is available only on Enterprise Support, including TA Priority on every plan
All AWS accounts get 56 checks, Business Support+ unlocks the full set, and TA Priority is reserved for Enterprise and Unified Operations
questions.explanation: All AWS accounts get 56 Trusted Advisor checks and Business Support+ and above unlock an additional 426 (482 total on AWS's check page, which elsewhere advertises 'more than 500'). Basic gets core checks: including all Service Limits checks and selected Security and Fault tolerance checks: so 'no checks at all' is false. TA Priority is an Enterprise and Unified Operations feature, not a Business Support+ one.

questions.question: A production team is comparing the four support plans in the 2026 lineup before renewing. Which statements about those plans are correct as of October 2026?
options: Business Support+ has a published monthly minimum of 29 USD per account
Enterprise Support includes a named Technical Account Manager
Business Support+ handles technical cases by phone, web and chat 24x7
Unified Operations carries a monthly minimum of 5,000 USD
Enterprise Support gives a first response under 5 minutes for a business-critical outage
Developer Support is available for new subscriptions as of October 2026
questions.explanation: Business Support+ costs a 29 USD monthly minimum per account with a 30-day minimum commitment and answers technical cases 24x7 by phone, web and chat, so the first and third statements hold. Enterprise Support includes a Technical Account Manager, so the second statement holds. The traps: the 50,000 USD monthly minimum with a 90-day commitment belongs to Unified Operations while Enterprise is 5,000 USD, so that option swaps in the Enterprise figure against the wrong plan (T6 numeric bait); the 5-minute first response comes from a Unified Operations Incident Management Engineer while Enterprise commits to under 15 minutes for a business-critical system down (T4 over-claim); and Developer Support stopped taking new subscriptions after 2 December 2025 and is discontinued 1 January 2027, so it is the stale-version trap. First response is a response, not a resolution, and AWS commits only to every reasonable effort.

questions.question: During an incident, a team follows the five-step drill used to decide whether the fault is theirs or AWS's. Put the steps in the order the drill walks them.
options: Check the CloudWatch alarm state for your own metric
Review Trusted Advisor for gaps in your own configuration
Subscribe to the AWS Health API before starting the triage
Open service health to look for a public AWS service event
Open your account health for account-specific issues
Raise a case in the AWS Support Center as the last resort
questions.explanation: Step 1 is CloudWatch: is my own metric breaching? Step 2, only if that is green, is Health service health, the public view that needs no sign-in and shows events that are not specific to an AWS account. Step 3 is Your account health for account-specific issues and scheduled changes. Step 4 is Trusted Advisor, when the gap is in my own configuration - it advises only and never enforces. Step 5 is a Support Center case, where the severity I choose sets the first-response clock, and on Basic Support no technical case can be opened at all. The Health API option is not a step: the dashboard is free for all customers while the AWS Health API requires Business Support+ (receiving health events through Amazon EventBridge is free), and skipping straight to step 5 fails on a free plan.

questions.question: Match each request a team needs to send to the AWS channel that actually handles it:
prompts: Ask a general how-to question such as tagging 400 instances
Report someone reselling a stolen machine image
Record a workload review with high-risk issues and milestones
Open an account-and-billing case about our own invoice
Have a partner open technical cases for our account
options: AWS Support Center console for account cases
AWS re:Post, the AWS managed community
AWS Partner-Led Support on an eligible plan
AWS Well-Architected Tool, available at no cost
AWS Trust and Safety team, separate from support
questions.explanation: A general how-to question belongs on AWS re:Post, the managed community with the Knowledge Center articles - it is not for time-sensitive or account-specific questions. Abuse such as a stolen image being resold goes to the AWS Trust and Safety team, which is separate from AWS Support. A workload review that captures high-risk issues, an improvement plan and a milestone is the Well-Architected Tool, and that tool costs nothing. An invoice problem with our own account is an account-and-billing case in the Support Center - Basic Support can open billing and account cases around the clock even though it cannot open technical cases. Partner-Led Support lets an eligible partner open cases on our behalf; Professional Services and solutions architects are engagement offerings, not case channels.

questions.question: A company wants AWS Health events pushed into its own on-call system through an API. What must be true for this to work?
options: Any plan works, because the AWS Health API is free to all customers
Business Support+ or above is required: the dashboard and EventBridge events are free to everyone, but the Health API is plan-gated
Only Unified Operations can use it, because it is part of incident detection
Basic Support is enough, because the Health Dashboard is included with Basic
questions.explanation: AWS states the Health Dashboard is available to all customers at no additional cost and that all customers can receive Health events through Amazon EventBridge free: but the AWS Health API requires Business Support+, Enterprise or Unified Operations. Confusing the free dashboard with the gated API is the standard trap in this task.

questions.question: An AWS announcement dated 1 October 2026 describes the AWS Well-Architected Agent (preview) as 'the next-gen evolution of AWS Trusted Advisor and the AWS Well-Architected Tool'. Which statement should govern your exam answers?
options: Answer with the AWS Well-Architected Agent, because every AWS announcement from 2026 is examinable
Trusted Advisor was retired on 1 October 2026, so its checks must be attributed to the Well-Architected Agent
The exam guide's service lists still name the AWS Well-Architected Tool and AWS Trusted Advisor and do not list the Agent, so key your answers to the guide, not to a preview
The Well-Architected Agent replaces the six pillars, so the pillar names no longer need memorising
